# Containers and orchestration {#sec-ch-ctr-containers}

> *"A virtual machine is taken to be an efficient, isolated duplicate of the
> real machine."* — Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg, 1974 [@popek1974]

```{python}
#| echo: false
import ctrbook as cb
cb.setup()
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- explain what a **container** is — a process with a restricted view of the
  machine, started from an **image** — and how it differs from a virtual
  machine and from a Python virtual environment;
- build "a container by hand" from the **kernel building blocks** —
  namespaces, a root filesystem, control groups, a union filesystem — and
  **prove** how the CPU is shared among containers by weights and quotas;
- read an **OCI image**: index, manifest, configuration, layers, digests;
  **prove** why content addressing with SHA-256 is safe in practice and why
  deleting a file in a later layer never shrinks an image (nor removes a
  secret);
- write **Dockerfiles** that build fast and small: **prove** the prefix
  property of the layer cache, compute the expected cost of a rebuild and the
  optimal order of the instructions, and use multi-stage builds;
- **run** containers correctly: ports, volumes, environment, users, limits,
  signals and exit codes (why `docker stop` sometimes takes ten seconds, what
  137 means);
- **orchestrate** containers with Kubernetes: deployments, services, probes,
  self-healing, scaling and rolling updates, with the bounds that govern them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
What containers are and what orchestration adds; the foundations of
containers; in practice, running a container with Docker and orchestrating a
container with Kubernetes.
:::

## What a container is, and what orchestration adds {#sec-ctr-what}

### The problem: "it works on my machine"

A program never runs alone. The phone book of Part I needs a Python
interpreter of the right version and nothing else; the house-price model of
Part III needs Python, NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn at versions that agree
with each other; the CRM of Part II needs a C++ standard library compatible
with the one it was compiled against. @sec-ch-venv solved part of the problem
for Python: a virtual environment isolates the **Python packages** of a
project, and pinning them in `requirements.txt` (@sec-requirements) makes
them reproducible. But a virtual environment does not contain the interpreter
itself, nor the system libraries the packages load (the C and Fortran
runtimes behind NumPy and SciPy, OpenSSL behind `https`), nor the operating
system's configuration. Move the project to another machine and any of these
can differ.

A **container image** packages *all* of it: a complete root filesystem — the
interpreter, the libraries, the code, the trained model — plus a little
metadata (which program to start, which port it listens on). A **container**
is a running instance of an image: an ordinary process of the host's kernel,
started with a restricted view of the machine — its own filesystem tree, its
own process numbers, its own network interfaces — and with limits on the
resources it can use. The image is to the container what a program file is to
a process (@sec-processes): a frozen description versus a running thing.

The name comes from shipping containers. Before them every cargo was loaded
differently; after them, cranes, ships and trucks handle one standard box and
do not care what is inside. A container image is the standard box of
software: the same image runs on a laptop, on a build server and on a cluster
of hundreds of machines, and the tools that move and run it do not care
whether it holds a web server or a neural network.

::: {#def-ctr-container}
## Image, container, runtime, engine, registry
- An **image** is an immutable, content-addressed bundle: an ordered list of
  filesystem **layers** plus a **configuration** (command, environment,
  user, exposed ports) (@sec-ctr-images).
- A **container** is a process tree started from an image, isolated by
  kernel **namespaces** and limited by **control groups** (@sec-ctr-kernel).
- A **runtime** creates containers from an unpacked image and a
  configuration (`runc`, implementing the OCI Runtime Specification
  [@oci2025runtime]).
- An **engine** (Docker Engine, containerd) builds, stores, moves and starts
  images and containers on one machine, calling the runtime.
- A **registry** stores images and serves them by name and digest (Docker
  Hub, GitHub Container Registry, a company's private registry).
:::

### Containers versus virtual machines

A **virtual machine** (VM) emulates a whole computer: a hypervisor gives each
VM virtual CPUs, memory and devices, and each VM boots its **own kernel**.
Popek and Goldberg stated in 1974 when an instruction set can be virtualised
efficiently — every instruction that could reveal or change the machine's
privileged state must trap to the hypervisor [@popek1974] — and modern CPUs
add hardware support to meet that condition. A container virtualises at a
higher level: **all containers share the host's kernel**, which merely shows
each of them a different view of its objects (files, processes, network).
Soltesz and colleagues called this *operating-system-based virtualisation*
and measured its advantage in density and speed [@soltesz2007]; Felter and
colleagues at IBM found containers within a few percent of native performance
on CPU, memory, storage and network benchmarks, while VMs paid noticeably on
I/O-heavy workloads [@felter2015].

| | Virtual machine | Container | Virtual environment (Part I) |
|---|---|---|---|
| What is isolated | a whole computer | a process tree's view of one kernel | the Python packages |
| Kernel | its own | the host's | the host's |
| Contains | OS, libraries, application | libraries, application (user space only) | Python packages only |
| Start-up | seconds (boot) | milliseconds to a second (start a process) | instant |
| Size | gigabytes | megabytes to a gigabyte | megabytes |
| Isolation strength | strong (hardware boundary) | weaker (shared kernel: a kernel bug affects all) | none |
| Runs another OS? | yes | only one with the same kernel (Linux images need a Linux kernel) | no |

The last row explains why Docker Desktop on macOS or Windows runs a small
Linux VM: Linux containers need a Linux kernel. The start-up time is easy to
measure: starting a container from an image that is already on disk means
creating the namespaces and cgroups and starting one process.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
import statistics, time
cb.run(f"docker run --rm {cb.LOCAL['ubuntu']} true")          # warm-up
_t = []
for _ in range(15):
    _s = time.perf_counter(); cb.run(f"docker run --rm {cb.LOCAL['ubuntu']} true"); _t.append(time.perf_counter() - _s)
startup_ms = 1000 * statistics.median(_t)
print(cb._fence("$ time docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 true      # median of 15 runs", ".bash"))
print(cb._output_block(f"{startup_ms:.0f} ms"))
```

On the machine that built this book (`{python} cb.machine()`) a container that
runs `true` and exits takes about `{python} f"{startup_ms:.0f}"` ms from
command to exit, including the round trips between the `docker` client, the
engine and the runtime. A VM boot takes seconds.

::: {.deep}
## History: from `chroot` to the OCI
Every piece of a container is older than Docker. **1979**: Version 7 Unix
adds `chroot`, which changes the root directory of a process — the first
"filesystem jail". **2000**: FreeBSD **jails** extend the idea to processes,
users and network addresses [@kamp2000]. **2004**: Solaris **Zones**.
**2002–2013**: Linux gains **namespaces** one at a time — mount (2002), UTS
and IPC (2006), PID (2008), network (2009), user (completed in 2013) — and
**control groups** (2007, first proposed as "process containers" by Paul
Menage and Rohit Seth at Google). **2008**: LXC combines them into a usable
tool. **2013**: Docker adds what was missing for developers — a simple image
format built from layers, a build file, and a registry to share images
[@merkel2014]. **2015**: Docker, CoreOS, Google and others found the **Open
Container Initiative**, which standardises the image format, the runtime and
the distribution protocol [@oci2025image; @oci2025runtime]; Kubernetes 1.0 is
released the same year, distilling a decade of Google's experience with its
internal cluster managers Borg and Omega [@verma2015; @burns2016].
:::

### What orchestration adds

One container on one machine is the beginning. A service in production runs
**many** copies of several containers on **many** machines, and something must
decide on which machine each copy runs, restart copies that crash, replace
machines that fail, route requests to healthy copies, add copies when the
load grows and replace old versions with new ones without interrupting the
service. **Orchestration** is the automation of these tasks; **Kubernetes** is
its dominant implementation. Its central idea, studied in @sec-ctr-k8s, is
**declarative**: you describe the desired state ("three copies of image X,
reachable under the name `scoring`") and control loops continuously compare it
with the observed state and act to close the gap.

## How the examples of this chapter run
Every command, build and manifest in this chapter was **executed** when the
book was built, by a small helper,
[`containers/ctrbook.py`](https://github.com/matteo-zirilli/ai-engineering-handbook/blob/main/containers/ctrbook.py),
which writes the files to a temporary directory, runs them, and replaces
container IDs, changing digests, temporary paths and durations with
placeholders such as `<id-1>` (equal values get equal placeholders). The build
machine could not reach public image registries, so every Dockerfile takes
its base image as a build argument — `ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim` followed by
`FROM ${BASE}` — and the book builds with `--build-arg BASE=<a local image>`
built from the Ubuntu 24.04 archive (with Python 3.12, as in the official
image); on your machine the default, official image is used and the commands
are exactly those shown. Measured times depend on the machine: the text uses
ratios and comparisons, which travel better than absolute numbers.
:::

## Kernel building blocks {#sec-ctr-kernel}

A container is not a kernel object: Linux has no "container" system call.
It is a **combination** of four independent mechanisms, each useful on its
own. This section takes them one at a time and then puts them together by
hand.

### Namespaces: a private view

A **namespace** wraps a global resource of the kernel so that the processes
inside it see their own isolated instance of the resource
[@linuxmanpages2025, namespaces(7)]. Each process belongs to exactly one
namespace of each type, inherited from its parent unless it asks for new ones
(the `clone` and `unshare` system calls).

| Namespace | Isolates | Effect inside a container |
|---|---|---|
| `mnt` | the list of mount points | its own filesystem tree |
| `uts` | host name and domain name | its own `hostname` |
| `ipc` | System V IPC, POSIX message queues | no shared memory with the host |
| `pid` | process IDs | its first process is PID 1; it cannot see the host's processes |
| `net` | network interfaces, routes, ports, firewall | its own `eth0`, its own port 8000 |
| `user` | user and group IDs, capabilities | root inside can be an unprivileged user outside |
| `cgroup` | the view of the cgroup hierarchy | sees its own cgroup as the root |
| `time` | the boot and monotonic clocks | rarely used by container engines |

The namespaces of a process are visible as links in `/proc/<pid>/ns`, whose
targets name the namespace by an inode number: two processes are in the same
namespace exactly when the numbers agree. Inside a container started by
Docker the effect is plain:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cb.sh(f"docker run --rm --hostname box {cb.LOCAL['ubuntu']} sh -c "
      "'echo \"my PID: $$, hostname: $(hostname)\"; echo \"processes I can see: $(ls /proc | grep -c \"^[0-9]\")\"'",
      shown="docker run --rm --hostname box ubuntu:24.04 sh -c 'echo \"my PID: $$, hostname: $(hostname)\"; "
            "echo \"processes I can see: $(ls /proc | grep -c \"^[0-9]\")\"'")
cb.sh("echo \"host: PID of this shell $$, hostname $(hostname), processes $(ls /proc | grep -c '^[0-9]')\"",
      shown="echo \"host: PID of this shell $$, hostname $(hostname), processes $(ls /proc | grep -c '^[0-9]')\"")
```

The shell inside is PID 1 and sees only itself and the few short-lived
processes of its own command line, while the host sees about a hundred
processes — among them, under an ordinary PID, the container's shell.

### A root filesystem: `chroot` and `pivot_root`

An image's filesystem is just a directory tree. `docker export` writes the
filesystem of a container as a tar archive, which we unpack into a directory
`rootfs/`; `chroot rootfs` then runs a program with `rootfs` as its `/`.
(Engines use the stronger `pivot_root` in a new mount namespace, which also
detaches the old root, but the effect on the program is the same.)

### A container by hand

With `unshare` — the command-line face of the system call — we can create new
namespaces and run a program in them. The flags below ask for new user, PID,
UTS and mount namespaces, map the current user to root inside, fork so that
the program becomes PID 1 of the new PID namespace, and mount a fresh `/proc`
inside the root filesystem:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
d = cb.project("handmade")
cb.sh(f"mkdir rootfs && docker export $(docker create {cb.LOCAL['ubuntu']} true) | tar -C rootfs -x && ls rootfs",
      cwd=d, shown="mkdir rootfs && docker export $(docker create ubuntu:24.04 true) | tar -C rootfs -x && ls rootfs")
cb.quiet("docker container prune -f")
cb.sh("unshare --user --map-root-user --pid --fork --uts --mount --mount-proc=rootfs/proc \\\n"
      "    chroot rootfs /bin/sh -c 'hostname box; echo \"PID $$, hostname $(hostname), user $(id -u)\"; "
      "ls /proc | grep -c \"^[0-9]\"; grep PRETTY /etc/os-release'", cwd=d)
cb.sh("hostname", cwd=d)
```

Inside: PID 1, host name `box`, user 0, the Ubuntu 24.04 userland of the
image and a `/proc` that lists only the container's processes. Outside, the
host name is unchanged. No daemon, no image format, no Docker: a container is
these kernel features applied to an ordinary process. What is still missing
is a limit on resources.

### Control groups: limits and accounting

A **control group** (cgroup) is a set of processes to which the kernel
applies resource **controllers**: `cpu` (how much CPU time), `memory` (how
much RAM; beyond the limit the kernel reclaims memory and, failing that, kills
a process of the group), `pids` (how many processes), `io` (disk bandwidth),
`cpuset` (which CPUs and memory nodes) [@linuxmanpages2025, cgroups(7)].
Cgroups form a hierarchy exposed as a filesystem under `/sys/fs/cgroup`;
moving a process into a group is writing its PID into the group's
`cgroup.procs` file.

There are two versions. **Version 1** (2007) has one hierarchy per controller
(`/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/…`, `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/…`); **version 2** (2016)
has a single unified hierarchy with consistent semantics [@heo2015] and is the
default on current distributions (Ubuntu since 21.10, Fedora since 31, Debian
since 11) and the one Kubernetes requires for new clusters (its support for
v1 is in maintenance mode and scheduled for removal). The
controls that matter for containers:

| Purpose | cgroup v2 file | cgroup v1 file | Docker flag |
|---|---|---|---|
| relative CPU weight | `cpu.weight` (1–10 000, default 100) | `cpu.shares` (2–262 144, default 1024) | `--cpu-shares` |
| CPU cap | `cpu.max` = `"quota period"` (default `max 100000`) | `cpu.cfs_quota_us`, `cpu.cfs_period_us` | `--cpus` |
| memory cap | `memory.max` | `memory.limit_in_bytes` | `--memory` |
| CPU set | `cpuset.cpus` | `cpuset.cpus` | `--cpuset-cpus` |

::: {.callout-important}
## This book was built on cgroup v1
The build machine uses cgroup **v1**, while almost every current host uses
v2. The text explains v2; the commands below print whichever files exist, and
the **numbers measured in this chapter come from v1** — the CPU scheduler
(CFS, and EEVDF in recent kernels) that enforces weights and quotas is the
same in both versions, so the ratios carry over.
:::

The flags of `docker run` translate directly into these files, which the
container can read from inside:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
_probe = ("for f in cpu.weight cpu.max memory.max cpu/cpu.shares cpu/cpu.cfs_quota_us cpu/cpu.cfs_period_us "
          "memory/memory.limit_in_bytes; do [ -f /sys/fs/cgroup/$f ] && echo \"$f = $(cat /sys/fs/cgroup/$f)\"; done")
cb.sh(f"docker run --rm --cpus=0.5 --cpu-shares=512 --memory=64m {cb.LOCAL['ubuntu']} sh -c '{_probe}'",
      shown=f"docker run --rm --cpus=0.5 --cpu-shares=512 --memory=64m ubuntu:24.04 sh -c '{_probe}'")
```

`--cpus=0.5` became a quota of 50 000 µs of CPU time per period of
100 000 µs; `--memory=64m` became a limit of $64 \times 2^{20}$ bytes;
`--cpu-shares=512` a relative weight. What do weights and quotas guarantee?

::: {#thm-ctr-cpu-share}
## CPU sharing by weights and quotas
Consider $m$ groups competing for a CPU capacity of $C$ (in CPUs) during an
interval of length $t$, and let $A$ be the set of groups that are
**backlogged** — always have runnable work — during the interval.

(i) If the scheduler is **weighted fair** (for any two groups $i, j$
backlogged on an interval, the CPU time they receive satisfies $S_i/S_j \ge
w_i/w_j$) and **work-conserving** (the CPU is never idle while some group has
work), then each backlogged group receives
$$
S_i = \frac{w_i}{\sum_{j \in A} w_j}\, C\, t .
$$ {#eq-ctr-share}
(ii) A group with quota $q$ per period $P$ receives at most
$q\lceil t/P\rceil$ CPU time in any interval of length $t$; in the long run
its rate is at most $q/P$ CPUs.
:::

*In one line:* weights matter only under contention and only among the
groups that want the CPU — idle groups' shares are redistributed to the busy
ones; quotas are hard caps that apply even on an idle machine.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-ctr-cpu-share
(i) This is the guarantee of **generalised processor sharing** (GPS), the
idealised fluid model of fair scheduling introduced by Parekh and Gallager for
network links [@parekh1993]; Linux's CFS and EEVDF schedulers approximate it
with a bounded lag. For $i, j \in A$, applying the fairness condition in both
directions gives $S_i/S_j \ge w_i/w_j$ and $S_j/S_i \ge w_j/w_i$, hence $S_i/S_j
= w_i/w_j$, i.e. $S_i = w_i\,\lambda$ for a common $\lambda$. Groups outside $A$
have no work at some moments; in the fully idle case they receive nothing,
and work conservation says the CPU is busy all the time, so $\sum_{i \in A}S_i
= Ct$. Then $\lambda\sum_{j \in A}w_j = Ct$, which gives @eq-ctr-share.
(If a non-backlogged group uses some CPU, the same argument applies to the
remaining capacity: the backlogged groups split it in proportion to their
weights.)

(ii) The bandwidth controller refills a budget of $q$ every period $P$ and
throttles the group when the budget is exhausted [@heo2015, "CPU"]; an
interval of length $t$ intersects at most $\lceil t/P\rceil$ periods, so the
group runs at most $q\lceil t/P\rceil$. Dividing by $t$ and letting $t \to
\infty$, $q\lceil t/P\rceil/t \to q/P$. $\blacksquare$
:::

When both mechanisms apply, the result is **water-filling**: capped groups
receive their cap, and the capacity they leave is shared by the others in
proportion to their weights. The widget computes the shares for three
containers on one CPU.

::: {.widget}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof cpuW = Inputs.form({
  a: Inputs.range([1, 10], {value: 2, step: 1, label: "weight of A"}),
  b: Inputs.range([1, 10], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "weight of B"}),
  c: Inputs.range([1, 10], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "weight of C"})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof cpuOn = Inputs.checkbox(["A", "B", "C"], {value: ["A", "B"], label: "busy containers"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof cpuCapA = Inputs.range([0.05, 1], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "cap of A (--cpus)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
cpuShares = {
  const w = {A: cpuW.a, B: cpuW.b, C: cpuW.c}, cap = {A: cpuCapA, B: 1, C: 1};
  let active = cpuOn.slice(), left = 1, out = {A: 0, B: 0, C: 0};
  // water-filling: give each active group its weighted share; fix those above their cap
  while (active.length) {
    const W = active.reduce((s, k) => s + w[k], 0);
    const over = active.filter(k => left * w[k] / W > cap[k] - out[k] + 1e-12);
    if (!over.length) { active.forEach(k => out[k] += left * w[k] / W); break; }
    over.forEach(k => { left -= cap[k] - out[k]; out[k] = cap[k]; });
    active = active.filter(k => !over.includes(k));
  }
  return ["A", "B", "C"].map(k => ({container: k, share: out[k]}));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-ctr-cpu-widget
//| fig-cap: "Share of one CPU received by each busy container under weighted fair, work-conserving scheduling (@thm-ctr-cpu-share). Idle containers get nothing and their share is redistributed; a cap on A (a quota) limits it even when the CPU would otherwise be free, and the rest goes to the others in proportion to their weights."
Plot.plot({
  height: 200, width: 460, marginLeft: 70, x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "share of the CPU", grid: true},
  y: {label: null},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(cpuShares, {y: "container", x: "share", fill: "container"}),
    Plot.text(cpuShares, {y: "container", x: "share", text: d => d.share.toFixed(3), dx: 22})
  ],
  color: {domain: ["A", "B", "C"], range: ["#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a"]}
})
```
:::

On cgroup v2, Docker's `--cpu-shares` (a v1 notion) must be converted into a
`cpu.weight`. Runtimes long used a linear map of the v1 range onto the v2
range, which turns the v1 default 1024 into a weight of 39 instead of 100;
since runc 1.3.2 and crun 1.23 they use a map that is quadratic in
$\log_2(\text{shares})$ and fixes the three points (2, 1), (1024, 100)
and (262 144, 10 000) [@holder2026]. Neither map preserves ratios
exactly, as a quick computation shows:

```{python}
import math

def weight_linear(shares):                     # runtimes before runc 1.3.2
    return 1 + ((shares - 2) * 9999) // 262142

def weight_quadratic(shares):                  # runc >= 1.3.2, crun >= 1.23
    L = math.log2(shares)
    return math.ceil(10 ** (L * L / 612 + 125 * L / 612 - 7 / 34))

for s in (512, 1024, 2048, 4096):
    print(f"cpu-shares {s:5d} -> weight {weight_linear(s):4d} (linear), {weight_quadratic(s):4d} (quadratic)")
r = weight_quadratic(2048) / weight_quadratic(1024)
print(f"2048:1024 becomes {r:.2f}:1 with the quadratic map")
```

So on a cgroup-v2 host with a current runtime, `--cpu-shares 2048` against
`1024` yields a ratio of about `{python} f"{weight_quadratic(2048) / weight_quadratic(1024):.2f}"`, not 2. If the exact
ratio matters, set the weights through the orchestrator's own resource model
(@sec-ctr-k8s) or read back the `cpu.weight` files.

### Union filesystems: layers without copies

Images are built in **layers** (@sec-ctr-images), and a container must see
them as one filesystem without copying them. A **union filesystem** — on
Linux, **overlayfs** — merges a stack of read-only *lower* directories with
one writable *upper* directory into a single view [@brown2014overlay]. Three
rules define it:

1. **Lookup**: a name resolves to the entry in the topmost layer that
   contains it.
2. **Copy-up**: modifying a file of a lower layer first copies it into the
   upper layer; the lower layer is never changed.
3. **Whiteout**: deleting a file that exists in a lower layer creates in the
   upper layer a **whiteout** — a character device with number 0/0 — that
   hides the name; the lower file is still there.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
d = cb.project("overlay")
cb.sh("mkdir lower upper work merged\n"
      "echo base > lower/a.txt && echo secret > lower/b.txt\n"
      "mount -t overlay overlay -o lowerdir=lower,upperdir=upper,workdir=work merged\n"
      "rm merged/b.txt && echo new > merged/c.txt\n"
      "echo '--- merged:' && ls merged && echo '--- upper:' && ls upper "
      "&& stat -c '%n is a %F, device number %t/%T' upper/b.txt && echo '--- lower:' && ls lower\n"
      "umount merged", cwd=d)
```

The merged view no longer shows `b.txt`, but the lower layer still holds it,
and the upper layer records its removal as a 0/0 device. Every running
container has its own upper directory on top of the image's layers: the
image is shared by all containers started from it, and what a container
writes disappears with it unless written to a volume (@sec-ctr-run).

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ctr1-kernel-easy}
## Easy — which namespaces change?
Print the targets of `/proc/self/ns/{user,pid,uts,mnt,net,ipc,cgroup}` on
the host and inside `unshare --user --map-root-user --pid --fork --uts
--mount-proc`. Predict first which ones will differ, then check.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`unshare` creates exactly the namespaces it is asked for; `--mount-proc`
needs a new mount namespace and asks for one implicitly. With `--fork`, the
child is the first process of the new PID namespace.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
_ns = "for n in user pid uts mnt net ipc cgroup; do echo \"$n $(readlink /proc/self/ns/$n)\"; done"
cb.sh(_ns, shown="for n in user pid uts mnt net ipc cgroup; do echo \"$n $(readlink /proc/self/ns/$n)\"; done   # host")
cb.sh(f"unshare --user --map-root-user --pid --fork --uts --mount-proc sh -c '{_ns}'")
```
`user`, `pid`, `uts` and `mnt` change; `net`, `ipc` and `cgroup` keep the
host's inode numbers because nobody asked for new ones — this "container"
shares the host's network, so a server it started would be reachable on the
host's ports. Docker asks for all of them (and, by default, not for a user
namespace — see @sec-ctr-run). The usual slip is to compare the *names* of
the links (`pid:`) rather than the numbers in brackets.
:::

::: {#exr-ctr1-kernel-medium}
## Medium — a container by hand, in Python
Write a Python function `container(rootfs, command, hostname, memory)` that
runs `command` in new user, PID, UTS and mount namespaces, chrooted into
`rootfs`, inside a fresh memory cgroup limited to `memory` bytes (support both
cgroup v1 and v2). Show that the command runs as PID 1 with the given host
name, and that a program allocating more than the limit is killed.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Create the cgroup directory, write the limit (`memory.max` on v2,
`memory/…/memory.limit_in_bytes` on v1), then start `unshare … chroot …` with
`subprocess.run(..., preexec_fn=...)` where the function writes
`os.getpid()` into the group's `cgroup.procs`: children inherit the cgroup.
A process killed by `SIGKILL` has `returncode == -9` in Python.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
import os, subprocess, uuid
from pathlib import Path

def container(rootfs, command, hostname="box", memory=None):
    """Run `command` (a shell string) in a hand-made container; return (returncode, output)."""
    cg = None
    if memory is not None:
        v2 = Path("/sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.controllers").exists()
        cg = Path("/sys/fs/cgroup" if v2 else "/sys/fs/cgroup/memory") / f"handmade-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}"
        cg.mkdir()
        (cg / ("memory.max" if v2 else "memory.limit_in_bytes")).write_text(str(memory))
        if v2:
            (cg / "memory.swap.max").write_text("0")              # no escape into swap
    def enter_cgroup():                                           # runs in the child, before exec
        if cg is not None:
            (cg / "cgroup.procs").write_text(str(os.getpid()))
    script = f"hostname {hostname}; {command}"
    proc = subprocess.run(["unshare", "--user", "--map-root-user", "--pid", "--fork", "--uts", "--mount",
                           f"--mount-proc={rootfs}/proc", "chroot", str(rootfs), "/bin/sh", "-c", script],
                          capture_output=True, text=True, preexec_fn=enter_cgroup)
    if cg is not None:
        cg.rmdir()                                                # empty again: the processes have exited
    return proc.returncode, (proc.stdout + proc.stderr).strip()

rootfs = cb.WORK / "handmade" / "rootfs"                          # unpacked from the image above
print(container(rootfs, 'echo "PID $$ on $(hostname)"', hostname="lab"))
fill = ("(s=$(head -c {n} /dev/zero | tr '\\0' x); echo held ${{#s}} bytes in a shell variable); "
        "echo exit status of the allocating subshell: $?")
print(container(rootfs, fill.format(n=10_000_000), memory=64 * 2**20))       # 10 MB: fits
print(container(rootfs, fill.format(n=150_000_000), memory=64 * 2**20))      # 150 MB: does not
```
The first call prints PID 1 and the chosen host name. A shell variable of
10 MB fits in the 64 MiB limit; one of 150 MB does not, and the kernel's OOM
killer terminates the subshell that holds it with `SIGKILL` — signal 9, which
the parent shell reports as $128 + 9 = 137$ (@sec-ctr-run). (Without the
subshell the victim would be a process that `unshare` waits for, and the
error would surface in a less readable way.) The function is, in miniature, what a
container runtime does — runc additionally uses `pivot_root`, drops
capabilities, applies seccomp filters and sets up the network. Typical
mistakes: writing the PID of the *parent* into `cgroup.procs` (then the
Jupyter kernel itself gets the limit), and forgetting that `rmdir` of a
cgroup fails while processes are still in it.
:::

::: {#exr-ctr1-kernel-hard}
## Hard — measure the CPU shares
Pin two CPU-bound containers to the same CPU (`--cpuset-cpus=0`), give them
`--cpu-shares` in ratio 2:1, and measure the work each does in the same time
window; compare with @eq-ctr-share. Then cap the heavier one with `--cpus=0.25`
and measure again; compare with water-filling. Finally, run one container
alone with `--cpus=0.5`: what fraction of the uncapped work does it do?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
"Work" can be the number of iterations of a busy loop. Start both
containers with `-d`, give them a common start time in the future (so that
the container start-up does not bias the window), and read the counts with
`docker logs`. Work done is proportional to CPU time received.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
import time

d = cb.project("cpushare")
cb.write(d, "burn.py", '''
    import sys, time
    start, T = float(sys.argv[1]), float(sys.argv[2])
    while time.time() < start:            # wait for the common start
        time.sleep(0.001)
    n, end = 0, start + T
    while time.time() < end:              # busy loop: count iterations
        for _ in range(1000):
            n += 1
    print(n)
''')

def burn(specs, T=5.0, cpuset="0"):
    """Run one container per spec (extra docker flags) on the same CPU; return the work counts."""
    start = time.time() + 3
    names = []
    for k, flags in enumerate(specs):
        name = f"burn{k}"
        cb.run(f"docker rm -f {name} >/dev/null 2>&1; docker run -d --name {name} --cpuset-cpus={cpuset} {flags} "
               f"-v {d}/burn.py:/burn.py:ro {cb.LOCAL['python']} python /burn.py {start} {T}")
        names.append(name)
    cb.run("docker wait " + " ".join(names))
    out = [int(cb.run(f"docker logs {n}").stdout) for n in names]
    cb.run("docker rm " + " ".join(names))
    return out

alone = burn([""])[0]
a, b = burn(["--cpu-shares=2048", "--cpu-shares=1024"])
print(f"weights 2:1   -> shares {a / (a + b):.3f} and {b / (a + b):.3f} (formula 0.667, 0.333); "
      f"total {(a + b) / alone:.3f} of one CPU")
a, b = burn(["--cpu-shares=2048 --cpus=0.25", "--cpu-shares=1024"])
print(f"A capped 0.25 -> shares {a / alone:.3f} and {b / alone:.3f} of one CPU (water-filling: 0.25, 0.75)")
half = burn(["--cpus=0.5"], cpuset="1")[0]
alone1 = burn([""], cpuset="1")[0]
print(f"alone, --cpus=0.5 -> {half / alone1:.3f} of the uncapped work")
capped_a, capped_b, half_ratio = a / alone, b / alone, half / alone1
```
The shares follow the weights closely and the total is about one CPU: the
scheduler is work-conserving. With the cap, the heavier container drops to
about a quarter of the CPU (`{python} f"{capped_a:.2f}"`) even though its
weight is larger, and the lighter one receives most of the rest
(`{python} f"{capped_b:.2f}"` against the 0.75 of water-filling). Alone, the
capped container does about half the work of an uncapped one
(`{python} f"{half_ratio:.2f}"` here) although the CPU is otherwise idle:
quotas are not work-conserving. Deviations of several percent, which change
from run to run, come from the scheduler's granularity, from the bandwidth
controller's accounting periods (a throttled container can overrun a period
slightly and then wait longer), and from the baseline and the capped runs not
seeing exactly the same machine — on a virtual machine the physical CPU is
shared with other tenants. These numbers are from cgroup v1 on a virtual machine; on a v2 host
with a current runtime, remember that `--cpu-shares 2048:1024` becomes a
weight ratio of about 1.74. Mistakes to avoid: measuring from container start
(start-up takes a sizeable fraction of a second and differs between the two),
and running on different CPUs, where there is no contention at all.
:::

## Images, layers and digests {#sec-ctr-images}

### The OCI image format

An image is not a disk image: it is a small set of JSON documents and tar
archives, all stored as **blobs** named by the SHA-256 hash of their content.
The **OCI Image Format Specification** [@oci2025image] defines four kinds of
document:

- a **layer** is a tar archive (usually gzip-compressed) of the files that a
  build step added, changed or deleted (deletions as whiteouts,
  @sec-ctr-kernel);
- the **configuration** is a JSON object with the command to run, the
  environment, the user, the working directory, the history of the build
  and the list `rootfs.diff_ids` — the digests of the *uncompressed* layers;
- the **manifest** lists the configuration and the layers by digest, size and
  media type;
- the **index** lists manifests, for instance one per CPU architecture
  (`linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`) of the same image.

A **digest** is the string `sha256:` followed by the 64 hexadecimal digits of
the SHA-256 hash of the blob's bytes [@nist2015]. Documents refer to each
other only by digest, so the structure is a directed acyclic graph of hashes
— a **Merkle DAG**, after Ralph Merkle's hash trees [@merkle1987]. To see it,
we build a tiny image — three lines, each explained in @sec-ctr-build; here
it is enough that each line that changes files adds a layer — and save it in
the OCI layout with `docker save`:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cb.reset_ids()
d = cb.project("tiny")
cb.show(d, "Dockerfile", """
    ARG BASE=ubuntu:24.04
    FROM ${BASE}
    COPY greeting.txt /greeting.txt
    RUN echo "built in a container" > /built.txt
    CMD ["cat", "/greeting.txt", "/built.txt"]
""")
cb.write(d, "greeting.txt", "hello from a layer\n")
cb.build(d, "local/tiny:1", args={"BASE": cb.LOCAL["ubuntu"]}, table=False, extra="--provenance=false")
cb.sh("docker run --rm local/tiny:1", shown="docker run --rm local/tiny:1")
cb.sh("mkdir oci && docker save local/tiny:1 | tar -C oci -x && ls oci && ls oci/blobs/sha256 | wc -l", cwd=d)
```

The layout has an `index.json`, an `oci-layout` marker and a directory of
blobs. A few lines of Python follow the graph from the index to the layers:

```{python}
import gzip, hashlib, json
from pathlib import Path

oci = cb.WORK / "tiny" / "oci"

def blob(digest):                              # "sha256:abc..." -> oci/blobs/sha256/abc...
    return oci / "blobs" / digest.replace(":", "/")

doc = json.loads((oci / "index.json").read_text())
while "manifests" in doc:                      # an index may point to another index
    print(doc["mediaType"].rsplit(".", 2)[-2], "->", len(doc["manifests"]), "entry")
    doc = json.loads(blob(doc["manifests"][0]["digest"]).read_text())
manifest = doc
config = json.loads(blob(manifest["config"]["digest"]).read_text())
print("manifest -> config of", manifest["config"]["size"], "bytes and", len(manifest["layers"]), "layers")
print("config: Cmd =", config["config"]["Cmd"], "| architecture =", config["architecture"])
for layer, diff_id in zip(manifest["layers"], config["rootfs"]["diff_ids"]):
    raw = blob(layer["digest"]).read_bytes()
    print(f"  layer: {len(raw):>10,} bytes compressed, {len(gzip.decompress(raw)):>11,} bytes as tar")

ok = all(hashlib.sha256(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest() == p.name for p in (oci / "blobs" / "sha256").iterdir())
print("every blob is named by the SHA-256 of its content:", ok)
```

The last line is the essence of **content addressing**: a name is not chosen,
it is computed from the bytes. Two consequences follow, and both rest on one
property of SHA-256.

::: {#thm-ctr-collision}
## Collision bound for content addressing
Model a hash with $b$-bit outputs as a function whose values on distinct
inputs are independent and uniform on $\{0, 1\}^b$. Among $n$ distinct
blobs, the probability that two of them get the same digest is at most
$$
\binom n2 2^{-b} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2^{b+1}} .
$$ {#eq-ctr-birthday}
For $b = 256$ and even $n = 2^{64} \approx 1.8 \times 10^{19}$ blobs it is
below $2^{-129} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-39}$.
:::

*In one line:* with 256-bit digests, an accidental collision is so unlikely
that "same digest" can be treated as "same bytes" — the bound grows only
with the *square* of the number of objects, the birthday effect, and $2^{256}$
absorbs any conceivable square.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-ctr-collision
For a pair $\{i, j\}$ of distinct blobs, $P(h_i = h_j) = \sum_v P(h_i =
v)P(h_j = v) = 2^b \cdot 2^{-2b} = 2^{-b}$. A collision is the union of the
$\binom n2$ events "$h_i = h_j$", so by the union bound (Boole's inequality)
its probability is at most $\binom n2 2^{-b}$. For $n = 2^{64}$:
$\binom n2 2^{-256} < 2^{128}\cdot 2^{-1}\cdot 2^{-256} = 2^{-129}$.
The bound is nearly tight while it is small: the classical birthday
computation gives $1 - \prod_{k<n}(1 - k2^{-b}) \approx 1 - e^{-n^2/2^{b+1}}$,
so collisions become likely only around $n \approx 2^{b/2} = 2^{128}$.
$\blacksquare$
:::

The model of the theorem is an idealisation: SHA-256 is a deterministic
function, specified in FIPS 180-4 [@nist2015], and what makes it safe is that
no one knows how to find two inputs with the same output faster than the
generic $\approx 2^{128}$ attempts of the birthday attack — the property
called **collision resistance**. The older SHA-1 lost it in practice in 2017
(the first public collision), which is why the OCI specification requires
SHA-256 or SHA-512 [@oci2025image, "Descriptors"].

::: {#prp-ctr-merkle}
## The top digest commits to everything
If no two distinct blobs reachable from an image share a digest, then two
images with the same manifest digest have the same configuration and the same
layers, byte for byte.
:::

*In one line:* checking one 64-digit digest checks the whole image, because a
change in any byte of any layer changes the layer's digest, hence the bytes
of the manifest that lists it, hence the manifest's digest.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ctr-merkle
By induction on the depth of the DAG. A blob with no children (a layer, a
configuration) is determined by its digest because distinct blobs have
distinct digests. A manifest is a blob, so equal digests mean equal manifest
bytes, hence equal lists of child digests, and by the induction hypothesis
equal children. The same argument applies to an index. $\blacksquare$
:::

This is what makes **pulling by digest** safe: `docker pull
python:3.12-slim@sha256:…` either receives exactly the image whose digest was
written down, or fails. Tags behave differently.

### Tags are mutable, digests are not

A **tag** (`local/app:v1`, `python:3.12-slim`) is a *name* that points to a
digest, and a name can be moved. Rebuilding with a change and reusing the tag
moves it silently:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cb.reset_ids()
id_before = cb.image_id("local/tiny:1")
cb.write(d, "greeting.txt", "hello again, from a new layer\n")
cb.build(d, "local/tiny:1", args={"BASE": cb.LOCAL["ubuntu"]}, table=False, extra="--provenance=false")
id_after = cb.image_id("local/tiny:1")
print(cb._output_block(cb.mask(f"before the rebuild local/tiny:1 -> {id_before}\nafter  the rebuild local/tiny:1 -> {id_after}")))
```

Anyone who deployed "`local/tiny:1`" yesterday and deploys it again today gets
a different image, with no error and no warning. Tags are for people;
**deployments should refer to digests** (or to tags that a process guarantees
never to move, such as a version that is published once).

### Layers add up

The union-filesystem rules of @sec-ctr-kernel have a direct consequence for
the size of an image.

::: {#prp-ctr-size}
## An image's size is the sum of its layers; deleting never shrinks it
The content of an image is the ordered list of its layers, and its size is the
sum of the layers' sizes. A step that deletes a file present in an earlier
layer adds a layer containing a whiteout; the earlier layer, and every byte of
the deleted file, remain part of the image and are downloaded by everyone who
pulls it.
:::

*In one line:* layers are append-only — a later step can hide a file, never
remove it.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ctr-size
By the OCI specification an image is its manifest, which lists *all* its
layers; layers are immutable blobs identified by their digests
(@prp-ctr-merkle), so no later step can change the bytes of an earlier one. A
deletion in step $k$ is recorded in layer $k$ as a whiteout entry
[@oci2025image, "Image Layer Filesystem Changeset"], which only changes how
the merged view resolves the name. Hence the set of stored bytes after step
$k$ contains those after step $k - 1$, and the size, the sum over the listed
layers, cannot decrease. $\blacksquare$
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
d = cb.project("bigfile")
cb.show(d, "Dockerfile", """
    ARG BASE=ubuntu:24.04
    FROM ${BASE}
    RUN head -c 50000000 /dev/urandom > /big.bin
    RUN rm /big.bin
""")
cb.build(d, "local/bigfile:1", args={"BASE": cb.LOCAL["ubuntu"]}, table=False)
_L = cb.layers("local/bigfile:1")
print("\n| Layer created by | Uncompressed size |\n|---|---:|")
for _l in _L:
    print(f"| `{cb._short(_l['created_by'], 55)}` | {_l['size'] / 1e6:,.1f} MB |")
print(f"| **total** | **{sum(_l['size'] for _l in _L) / 1e6:,.1f} MB** |\n")
```

The 50 MB of random bytes (incompressible, so they cost 50 MB of download too)
are in the image for ever, although no container will ever see them. The
remedy is to create and delete temporary files **in the same step** (`RUN
download && use && rm`), or to build in one stage and copy only the result
into another (@sec-ctr-build). The same mechanism makes **secrets** copied into
an image and deleted later recoverable by anyone who can pull it
(@exr-ctr1-images-hard).

### Reproducible images

An image is **reproducible** if building the same sources twice gives the same
digest. It is the strongest form of "pinning": a third party can rebuild the
image and check, by comparing one digest, that it was built from the claimed
sources. By default two builds of the same Dockerfile differ:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cb.reset_ids()
d = cb.project("repro")
cb.show(d, "Dockerfile", """
    ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim
    FROM ${BASE}
    COPY app.py /app/app.py
    CMD ["python", "/app/app.py"]
""")
cb.write(d, "app.py", 'print("same sources, same image?")\n')
for _k in (1, 2):
    cb.build(d, f"local/repro:{_k}", extra="--no-cache", table=False, show_cmd=False)
print(cb._fence("$ docker build --no-cache -t local/repro:1 .   # and again, -t local/repro:2", ".bash"))
print(cb._output_block(cb.mask(f"local/repro:1 {cb.image_id('local/repro:1')}\nlocal/repro:2 {cb.image_id('local/repro:2')}")))
```

The file contents are identical; what differs is **time**: the files' modification
times inside the layer, the `created` dates in the configuration and its
history, and the provenance attestation that BuildKit attaches by default. The
reproducible-builds project standardised a remedy, the environment variable
`SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`, a fixed timestamp that tools use instead of the clock
[@reproduciblebuilds2017]; BuildKit honours it for the image metadata and can
rewrite the timestamps of the files in the layers:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
for _k in (3, 4):
    cb.build(d, f"local/repro:{_k}", table=False, show_cmd=False,
             extra=f"--no-cache --provenance=false --build-arg SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=0 "
                   f"--output type=image,name=local/repro:{_k},rewrite-timestamp=true")
print(cb._fence("$ docker build --no-cache --provenance=false --build-arg SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=0 \\\n"
                "    --output type=image,name=local/repro:3,rewrite-timestamp=true .      # and again, :4", ".bash"))
print(cb._output_block(cb.mask(f"local/repro:3 {cb.image_id('local/repro:3')}\nlocal/repro:4 {cb.image_id('local/repro:4')}")))
```

Same placeholder, same digest. Real images need more care, because every
input must be pinned: the **base image by digest** (`FROM
python:3.12-slim@sha256:…`), the **packages by version and hash** (`pip
install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt`, @sec-requirements), and every
step must be deterministic — no unpinned `apt-get install`, no downloads of
"latest", no random seeds left free, no compilation of `.pyc` files that embed
timestamps (`pip install --no-compile`, or `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE`).
@exr-ctr1-reproducible applies this to the model image.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ctr1-images-easy}
## Easy — find a layer by its hash
Take the layer of `local/tiny:1` that contains `greeting.txt`. Compute by hand
(with `sha256sum` or `hashlib`) the digest of the compressed blob and of the
uncompressed tar, and find each in the image: the first among the blobs and
the manifest, the second in the configuration's `diff_ids`. Then use
@eq-ctr-birthday to bound the probability of a collision among $10^{12}$
blobs — more than all the images ever pushed to public registries.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
The layers are listed in the manifest in build order; the configuration's
`history` says which step produced each (entries with `empty_layer` produce
none). `gzip.decompress` gives the tar bytes.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
oci = cb.WORK / "tiny" / "oci"
cb.run("rm -rf oci && mkdir oci && docker save local/tiny:1 | tar -C oci -x", cwd="tiny")   # the rebuilt image
doc = json.loads((oci / "index.json").read_text())
while "manifests" in doc:
    doc = json.loads(blob(doc["manifests"][0]["digest"]).read_text())
config = json.loads(blob(doc["config"]["digest"]).read_text())
steps = [h.get("created_by", "(base image)") for h in config["history"] if not h.get("empty_layer")]
k = next(i for i, s in enumerate(steps) if "greeting" in s)        # the COPY step
raw = blob(doc["layers"][k]["digest"]).read_bytes()
compressed = "sha256:" + hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest()
uncompressed = "sha256:" + hashlib.sha256(gzip.decompress(raw)).hexdigest()
print("step:", steps[k])
print("compressed digest listed in the manifest:   ", compressed == doc["layers"][k]["digest"])
print("uncompressed digest listed in the diff_ids: ", uncompressed == config["rootfs"]["diff_ids"][k])
n = 10 ** 12
print(f"collision bound for 1e12 blobs: {n * (n - 1) / 2 ** 257:.1e}")
```
The two digests differ because they hash different bytes: the manifest refers
to what travels and is stored (compressed), the configuration to what is
unpacked (so that recompressing a layer with another tool does not change the
image's identity as seen by the runtime). The bound is about $4 \times
10^{-54}$: the probability of an accidental collision is not a practical
concern; a deliberate one would require breaking SHA-256. A frequent mistake
is to hash the file *inside* the layer instead of the layer's tar.
:::

::: {#exr-ctr1-images-medium}
## Medium — an inspector for the OCI layout
Write `inspect_oci(path)` that walks an OCI layout (the output of `docker
save`, unpacked) from `index.json` to the layers and prints, for each layer,
the step that created it, its compressed and uncompressed sizes, the number
of files it adds and the whiteouts it contains (as the paths they delete).
Run it on `local/bigfile:1`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`tarfile.open(fileobj=io.BytesIO(data))` reads a tar from memory. In the OCI
layer format a whiteout for `dir/name` is a file named `dir/.wh.name`;
`.wh..wh..opq` marks an "opaque" directory whose lower contents are hidden.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
import io, tarfile

def inspect_oci(path):
    path = Path(path)
    def blob(dg):
        return path / "blobs" / dg.replace(":", "/")
    doc = json.loads((path / "index.json").read_text())
    while "manifests" in doc:                                   # index -> (index ->) manifest
        doc = json.loads(blob(doc["manifests"][0]["digest"]).read_text())
    config = json.loads(blob(doc["config"]["digest"]).read_text())
    steps = [h.get("created_by", "(base)") for h in config["history"] if not h.get("empty_layer")]
    print(f"{'step':<42} {'compressed':>11} {'tar':>12} {'files':>7}  whiteouts")
    for step, layer in zip(steps, doc["layers"]):
        raw = blob(layer["digest"]).read_bytes()
        data = gzip.decompress(raw) if raw[:2] == b"\x1f\x8b" else raw
        with tarfile.open(fileobj=io.BytesIO(data)) as tar:
            members = tar.getmembers()
        wh = [m.name.replace(".wh.", "") for m in members if Path(m.name).name.startswith(".wh.")]
        files = sum(m.isfile() for m in members) - len(wh)          # whiteouts are stored as empty files
        label = step.replace("/bin/sh -c ", "")[:42]
        print(f"{label:<42} {len(raw):>11,} {len(data):>12,} {files:>7}  {wh}")

cb.run("rm -rf oci && mkdir oci && docker save local/bigfile:1 | tar -C oci -x", cwd="bigfile")
inspect_oci(cb.WORK / "bigfile" / "oci")
```
The third layer adds one file of 50 MB; the fourth adds no file and one
whiteout, `big.bin`. The compressed size of the random file is about its
real size — random bytes do not compress — while the base layer shrinks by
half. The inspector does in thirty lines what tools such as `dive` or `crane`
do; the typical slip is to assume that every layer is gzip-compressed
(uncompressed and zstd layers are allowed: check the media type or the magic
bytes).
:::

::: {#exr-ctr1-images-hard}
## Hard — a secret that will not go away
A Dockerfile copies a file with an API token into the image, uses it in a
`RUN` step and deletes it with `RUN rm`. Show that the token can be recovered
from the image with nothing but `docker save` and Python. Then fix the
Dockerfile twice — with a multi-stage build and with a BuildKit secret mount
(`RUN --mount=type=secret,...`) — and verify, by scanning every layer, that
the token has gone.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Scan the decompressed bytes of every layer for the token. With a secret mount
the file is visible only during the `RUN` step, at `/run/secrets/<id>`, and
is never written to a layer; build with `--secret id=token,src=token.env`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| output: asis
TOKEN = "TOKEN=sk-demo-0123456789abcdef"

def layers_containing(tag, needle):
    """Indices of the layers of `tag` whose tar contains `needle`."""
    out = cb.WORK / f"scan-{tag.replace('/', '_').replace(':', '_')}"
    cb.run(f"rm -rf {out} && mkdir {out} && docker save {tag} | tar -C {out} -x")
    def blob(dg):
        return out / "blobs" / dg.replace(":", "/")
    doc = json.loads((out / "index.json").read_text())
    while "manifests" in doc:
        doc = json.loads(blob(doc["manifests"][0]["digest"]).read_text())
    hits = []
    for i, layer in enumerate(doc["layers"]):
        raw = blob(layer["digest"]).read_bytes()
        if needle.encode() in (gzip.decompress(raw) if raw[:2] == b"\x1f\x8b" else raw):
            hits.append(i)
    return hits

d = cb.project("secret")
cb.write(d, "token.env", TOKEN + "\n")
cb.files(d, {"Dockerfile.leaky": """
    ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim
    FROM ${BASE}
    COPY token.env /tmp/token.env
    RUN . /tmp/token.env && echo "using a token of ${#TOKEN} characters" && rm /tmp/token.env
""", "Dockerfile.multistage": """
    ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim
    FROM ${BASE} AS fetch
    COPY token.env /tmp/token.env
    RUN . /tmp/token.env && echo "a result obtained with the token" > /result.txt
    FROM ${BASE}
    COPY --from=fetch /result.txt /result.txt
""", "Dockerfile.secret": """
    ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim
    FROM ${BASE}
    RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token . /run/secrets/token && echo "a result obtained with the token" > /result.txt
"""})
cb.build(d, "local/secret:leaky", dockerfile="Dockerfile.leaky", table=False)
cb.build(d, "local/secret:multistage", dockerfile="Dockerfile.multistage", table=False)
cb.build(d, "local/secret:mount", dockerfile="Dockerfile.secret", table=False, extra="--secret id=token,src=token.env")
print("\n| Image | Layers containing the token |\n|---|---|")
for tag in ("local/secret:leaky", "local/secret:multistage", "local/secret:mount"):
    print(f"| `{tag}` | {layers_containing(tag, TOKEN) or 'none'} |")
```
In the leaky image the `COPY` layer still holds the token in clear text,
although the file is absent from every container (@prp-ctr-size): anyone who
can pull the image can read it. In the multi-stage build the token exists only
in the first stage, which is not part of the final image; with the secret
mount it is never written to any layer. The scan is the verification that
matters — "the file is not there when I run the container" proves nothing. In
a real project add a check like `layers_containing` to the CI pipeline, keep
secrets out of the build context with `.dockerignore`, and **rotate** any
secret that was ever pushed in an image: deleting the tag does not delete
copies already pulled. Note also that `ARG` and `ENV` values are stored in
the image configuration — passing a secret as a build argument leaks it too.
:::

## Building images {#sec-ctr-build}

### The running example: a model in a container

From here on the examples serve a small **model in production**: a
classifier of the three wine cultivars of the wine data
[@aeberhard1992], a scikit-learn pipeline — standardisation and logistic
regression, scaler inside the pipeline as @sec-leakage requires — trained
when the image is built, saved with `joblib`, and served over HTTP. The
server uses only the standard library; Part VI replaces it with a proper API
framework. The pinned requirements and the two programs:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
d = cb.scoring("scoring", show_files=("requirements.txt", "train.py", "serve.py"))
```

`joblib.dump` writes the fitted pipeline to a file (a pickle, with efficient
storage of NumPy arrays) and `joblib.load` reads it back: the model is trained
once and loaded by every container that serves it. A pickle can execute code
when loaded, so load only files you produced — here, files produced at build
time inside the image.

### Anatomy of a Dockerfile

A **Dockerfile** is a list of instructions executed in order, each on top of
the result of the previous one [@docker2026, "Dockerfile reference"]:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cb.show(d, "Dockerfile")
```

| Instruction | Effect | Creates a layer? |
|---|---|---|
| `ARG BASE=…` | a build-time variable with a default; overridable with `--build-arg` | no |
| `FROM image` | the base image: its layers become the first layers | (inherits) |
| `WORKDIR /app` | the directory for the following instructions and for the container | yes (empty) |
| `COPY src dst` | copies files from the **build context** into the image | yes |
| `RUN command` | runs a command in a temporary container; the changes become a layer | yes |
| `ENV`, `USER`, `EXPOSE`, `CMD`, `ENTRYPOINT` | set fields of the configuration | no |

`CMD ["python", "serve.py"]` is the **exec form**, a JSON array run directly;
`CMD python serve.py` is the **shell form**, run as `/bin/sh -c "python
serve.py"` — a difference that matters for signals (@sec-ctr-run). `EXPOSE`
only documents the port; publishing it is a decision taken at `docker run`.

The **build context** is the directory given to `docker build` (here `.`):
`COPY` can only read from it, and the builder receives from it the files the
`COPY` instructions need. A `.dockerignore` file lists paths to leave out —
data sets, virtual environments, `.git`, secrets — so that a `COPY . .` can
never bring them into the image (@exr-ctr1-build-medium).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
secs_cold, _ = cb.build(d, "local/scoring:1", extra="--no-cache")
```

The first build, from scratch (`--no-cache`), ran every step
(`{python} f"{secs_cold:.0f}"` s here, almost all of it installing the
packages). Building again, without changes, takes a
fraction of a second, because of the **layer cache**:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
secs_warm, _ = cb.build(d, "local/scoring:1")
```

### The layer cache

Before executing an instruction, the builder computes a **cache key** from the
key of the previous step, the instruction's text and, for `COPY`, a checksum
of the copied files; if a layer with that key exists, it is reused
[@docker2026, "Build cache"]. Formally, with $k_0$ the base image's digest and
$H$ a hash function,
$$
k_i = H\big(k_{i-1},\ \text{instruction}_i,\ \text{inputs}_i\big),\qquad i = 1, \dots, m .
$$ {#eq-ctr-cache-key}
Change one character of `serve.py` and rebuild:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
(d / "serve.py").write_text((d / "serve.py").read_text().replace("keep the logs quiet", "silence the access log"))
secs_code, _ = cb.build(d, "local/scoring:1")
```

Only the last `COPY` ran again (`{python} f"{secs_code:.1f}"` s). Change the
requirements instead, and everything after them runs again — including the
training, whose inputs did not change.

::: {#thm-ctr-prefix}
## Prefix property of the layer cache
With cache keys defined by @eq-ctr-cache-key, step $i$ is taken from the cache
only if none of the steps $1, \dots, i$ (nor the base image) has changed since
a build that stored its key. Consequently, if the first changed step is $j$,
then exactly the steps $j, j + 1, \dots, m$ are executed.
:::

*In one line:* the cache is a chain — break one link and every link after it
must be rebuilt, however unchanged it is itself.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-ctr-prefix
By induction on $i$, $k_i$ is a function of $(k_0, \text{instruction}_1,
\text{inputs}_1, \dots, \text{instruction}_i, \text{inputs}_i)$. If any of
these changed, then — barring a collision of $H$, negligible by
@thm-ctr-collision — $k_i$ is a value never stored before, and step $i$ must
run. Conversely, if none changed, $k_i$ equals a stored key and the stored
layer is reused. If $j$ is the first changed step, the inputs of steps $< j$
are unchanged, so they are reused, and every $k_i$ with $i \ge j$ depends on
the changed step, so they all run. $\blacksquare$
:::

The prefix property turns the order of the instructions into an
optimisation problem. Suppose that between two builds step $i$ changes with
probability $p_i$, independently of the others, and costs $c_i$ seconds to
execute.

::: {#thm-ctr-cost}
## Expected cost of a rebuild, and the optimal order
(i) The expected time of a rebuild is
$$
\mathbb E[C] = \sum_{i=1}^m c_i\Big[1 - \prod_{j \le i}(1 - p_j)\Big] .
$$ {#eq-ctr-cost}
(ii) If the steps can be put in any order (no step needs the result of
another), the expected cost is minimised by sorting them by increasing
$$
r_i = \frac{p_i}{(1 - p_i)\,c_i} ,
$$ {#eq-ctr-order}
with steps that always change ($p_i = 1$) last: expensive, rarely changing
steps first; cheap, often changing steps last.
:::

*In one line:* each step pays its cost with the probability that something
up to it changed; and an exchange argument shows that the best order puts the
"stable and expensive" steps early.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-ctr-cost
(i) By @thm-ctr-prefix, step $i$ runs if and only if at least one of the
steps $1, \dots, i$ changed. By independence, the probability that none
changed is $\prod_{j \le i}(1 - p_j)$. With $X_i$ the indicator that step $i$
runs, $C = \sum_ic_iX_i$, and linearity of expectation gives @eq-ctr-cost.

(ii) **Exchange argument.** Take an order and two adjacent steps $a, b$ at
positions $i, i + 1$; let $Q = \prod_{j < i}(1 - p_j)$ and $q = 1 - p$.
Swapping them changes only the terms of positions $i$ and $i + 1$:
$$
\underbrace{c_a(1 - Qq_a) + c_b(1 - Qq_aq_b)}_{a\text{ first}} -
\underbrace{\big[c_b(1 - Qq_b) + c_a(1 - Qq_aq_b)\big]}_{b\text{ first}}
= Q\,\big(c_bq_b\,p_a - c_aq_a\,p_b\big),
$$
so putting $a$ first is at least as good if and only if $c_bq_bp_a \le
c_aq_ap_b$, that is $r_a \le r_b$ (when $q_a, q_b > 0$; a step with $q = 0$
should come after any step with $q > 0$, since then the difference has the
sign of $-c_aq_ap_b \le 0$ with $a$ the step with $q_a > 0$). Any order that is
not sorted by $r$ has an adjacent pair out of order; swapping it does not
increase the cost. Repeating the swap (bubble sort) reaches the sorted order
in finitely many steps without ever increasing the cost, so the sorted order
is optimal. $\blacksquare$
:::

The criterion is a ratio, and its consequences match the folklore of
Dockerfiles: install dependencies (expensive, rarely changed) before copying
the code (cheap, changed at every commit); copy `requirements.txt` alone
before `pip install`, rather than the whole project. The widget compares two
orders of the steps of the scoring image.

```{python}
#| echo: false
_step_costs = {"install packages": max(secs_cold - 2, 1.0), "train the model": 1.5, "copy the code": 0.2}
ojs_define(ctrCosts=_step_costs)
```

::: {.widget}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ctrP = Inputs.form({
  deps: Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.05, step: 0.01, label: "P(requirements change)"}),
  train: Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.10, step: 0.01, label: "P(training code changes)"}),
  code: Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.80, step: 0.01, label: "P(server code changes)"})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ctrOrders = {
  const steps = {deps: ["install packages", ctrCosts["install packages"], ctrP.deps],
                 train: ["train the model", ctrCosts["train the model"], ctrP.train],
                 code: ["copy the code", ctrCosts["copy the code"], ctrP.code]};
  const cost = order => { let none = 1, total = 0, rows = [];
    for (const k of order) { const [name, c, p] = steps[k]; none *= (1 - p);
      rows.push({step: name, cost: c, prob: 1 - none}); total += c * (1 - none); }
    return {rows, total}; };
  const good = cost(["deps", "train", "code"]), bad = cost(["code", "train", "deps"]);
  return [...good.rows.map(r => ({...r, order: `deps → train → code (E[C] = ${good.total.toFixed(1)} s)`})),
          ...bad.rows.map(r => ({...r, order: `code → train → deps (E[C] = ${bad.total.toFixed(1)} s)`}))];
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-ctr-cache-widget
//| fig-cap: "Probability that each step of the scoring image is rebuilt (@eq-ctr-cost), for the recommended order and the reverse one; the legend gives the expected rebuild time E[C]. Step costs were measured on the build machine; the change probabilities are yours to set."
Plot.plot({
  height: 240, width: 560, marginLeft: 120, x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "P(step is rebuilt)", grid: true},
  fy: {label: null}, y: {label: null},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [Plot.barX(ctrOrders, {y: "step", x: "prob", fill: "order", fy: "order"})]
})
```
:::

### Multi-stage builds

A **multi-stage** Dockerfile has several `FROM` instructions; each starts a
stage, and `COPY --from=<stage>` copies files from an earlier stage. Only the
last stage becomes the image. The classic use is to **compile in a full
toolchain and ship only the result**. A C++ program linked statically
(`-static` copies the C and C++ libraries into the executable, @sec-toolchain)
needs nothing at all at run time, so its final stage can start `FROM
scratch`, the empty image:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
d = cb.project("cpp-static")
cb.files(d, {"hello.cpp": """
    #include <iostream>
    #include <string>

    int main(int argc, char** argv) {
        std::string who = argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "world";
        std::cout << "hello, " << who << ", from a static binary\\n";
    }
""", "Dockerfile": """
    ARG BUILDER=gcc:13
    FROM ${BUILDER} AS build
    WORKDIR /src
    COPY hello.cpp .
    RUN g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -static -o hello hello.cpp

    FROM scratch
    COPY --from=build /src/hello /hello
    ENTRYPOINT ["/hello"]
"""})
cb.build(d, "local/hello-static:1", table=False)
cb.sh("docker run --rm local/hello-static:1 container")
_static = sum(l["size"] for l in cb.layers("local/hello-static:1"))
_builder = sum(l["size"] for l in cb.layers(cb.LOCAL["gcc"]))
print(cb._output_block(f"final image: {_static / 1e6:.1f} MB    build stage's base image: {_builder / 1e6:.0f} MB"))
```

The final image holds one file of about `{python} f"{_static / 1e6:.1f}"` MB; the
compiler image it was built in is more than a hundred times larger and is
not shipped. For Python the gain is smaller — the interpreter and the
libraries are needed at run time — but a build stage still keeps compilers,
test tools, caches and training data out of the final image
(@exr-ctr1-build-hard). A second use, seen in @exr-ctr1-images-hard, is to
keep **secrets** out of the final image; BuildKit's secret mounts
(`RUN --mount=type=secret`) do it without a second stage.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ctr1-build-easy}
## Easy — predict the rebuild
Two orders of the scoring Dockerfile are proposed: (A) the one above —
requirements, `pip install`, `train.py`, training, server code; (B) `COPY . .`
first, then `pip install`, then training. For each order, which steps are
rebuilt when (1) `serve.py` changes, (2) `requirements.txt` changes, (3)
nothing changes but the build machine's cache was emptied? Answer by hand
with @thm-ctr-prefix, then check (1) for order B by building it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
In order B the `COPY . .` step's inputs include *every* file of the context,
so any change to any file changes its key.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(1) A: only `COPY serve.py score.py`. B: everything after the base image —
`COPY . .` changed, so the installation (about
`{python} f"{secs_cold:.0f}"` s) and the training run again for a one-line change.
(2) A and B: everything from the copy of the requirements on. (3) Both:
everything; the cache helps only if it is there (CI machines often start
empty — export and import the cache, e.g. `--cache-from`/`--cache-to`).
```{python}
#| output: asis
d = cb.scoring("order-b", dockerfile="""
    ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim
    FROM ${BASE}
    WORKDIR /app
    COPY . .
    RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
    RUN python train.py
    CMD ["python", "serve.py"]
""", show_files=("Dockerfile",))
cb.build(d, "local/scoring:b", show_cmd=False, table=False)                 # fill the cache
(d / "serve.py").write_text((d / "serve.py").read_text() + "# a comment\n")
cb.build(d, "local/scoring:b")
```
Order B re-installs scikit-learn because a comment changed in the server.
The usual mistake is believing that Docker "knows" that `pip install` does not
read `serve.py`: the cache key cannot know what a command reads, only what was
copied before it.
:::

::: {#exr-ctr1-build-medium}
## Medium — measure the order and the context
Measure the rebuild time after a change of `serve.py` for orders A and B
(three repetitions each). Then put a 200 MB file `data/raw.bin` in the build
context and measure how the size of the context sent to the builder and the
build time change with and without a `.dockerignore` that excludes `data/`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`docker build --progress=plain` prints a line `transferring context: … MB`
for the context. Use random bytes for the data file, so that compression in
transit cannot hide its size.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
import re, time, statistics

def rebuild_after_edit(d, tag, n=3):
    """Median time of n rebuilds, each after a one-line edit of serve.py."""
    times = []
    for k in range(n):
        (d / "serve.py").write_text((d / "serve.py").read_text() + f"# edit {k} {time.time()}\n")
        secs, _ = cb.build(d, tag, show_cmd=False, table=False)   # docker build with the local base image
        times.append(secs)
    return statistics.median(times)

dA = cb.scoring("medium-a"); cb.build(dA, "local/scoring:ma", show_cmd=False, table=False)
dB = cb.WORK / "order-b"
print(f"rebuild after editing serve.py: order A {rebuild_after_edit(dA, 'local/scoring:ma'):.1f} s, "
      f"order B {rebuild_after_edit(dB, 'local/scoring:b'):.1f} s (median of 3)")

def context_size(d):
    """Build once and read from BuildKit's log how many MB of context were transferred."""
    secs, _ = cb.build(d, "local/scoring:ctx", show_cmd=False, table=False)
    sizes = re.findall(r"load build context\n#\d+ transferring context: ([\d.]+)(kB|MB|GB|B)", cb.LAST_BUILD_LOG)
    val, unit = sizes[-1]
    return float(val) * {"B": 1e-6, "kB": 1e-3, "MB": 1, "GB": 1e3}[unit], secs

for d_, label in ((dA, "order A (COPY of named files)"), (dB, "order B (COPY . .)")):
    (d_ / "data").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (d_ / "data" / "raw.bin").write_bytes(np.random.default_rng(0).bytes(200_000_000))
    (d_ / ".dockerignore").unlink(missing_ok=True)
    image_mb = lambda: sum(l["size"] for l in cb.layers("local/scoring:ctx")) / 1e6
    big, t_big = context_size(d_); size_big = image_mb()
    (d_ / ".dockerignore").write_text("data/\n.git/\n__pycache__/\n*.env\n")
    small, t_small = context_size(d_); size_small = image_mb()
    print(f"{label}: context {big:7.2f} MB without .dockerignore, {1000 * small:5.1f} kB with it; "
          f"image {size_big:.0f} MB without it, {size_small:.0f} MB with it")
```
Order A rebuilds in well under a second, order B in the time of a full
installation. The context measurement holds a surprise: with order A the
200 MB file never travels, with or without `.dockerignore`, because BuildKit
transfers only the paths that the `COPY` instructions name. With `COPY . .`
everything travels **and ends up in the image** — 200 MB of data shipped to
every server that pulls it — unless `.dockerignore` excludes it. So the
ignore file matters exactly when the Dockerfile copies whole directories,
which is also when it protects against copying secrets, `.git` and
virtual environments into the image. Mistake to avoid: timing a single
build — the first one after an edit may include unrelated work, such as
garbage collection of the cache.
:::

::: {#exr-ctr1-build-hard}
## Hard — the optimal order for the scoring image
For the scoring image, take as steps (1) installing the packages, (2) copying
and running the training, (3) copying the server code, with the costs measured
above and change probabilities per commit $p = (0.05, 0.10, 0.80)$. (a) Compute
@eq-ctr-cost for all six orders and check that @eq-ctr-order picks the best.
(b) Verify the formula by simulating 10 000 commits. (c) Check one prediction
with real builds. (d) Reduce the image's size with a multi-stage build that
installs the packages into a virtual environment in a first stage, trains the
model there, and copies only the environment, the model and the server into
the final stage; measure the gain.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
For (b), draw for each commit which steps changed, rebuild from the first
changed step with the cost of every step from there on, and average. For
(d), install the packages into a directory of their own in the build stage
(`pip install --target=/deps`), delete what serving does not need — the test
suites that NumPy, SciPy and scikit-learn ship, `__pycache__` directories —
and copy only that directory into the final stage, with `ENV
PYTHONPATH=/deps`. A virtual environment (@sec-venv-internals) would also
work, but it carries its own copy of `pip`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from itertools import permutations

names = ["install", "train", "code"]
c = np.array([max(secs_cold - 2, 1.0), 1.5, 0.2])         # seconds; install measured above
p = np.array([0.05, 0.10, 0.80])

def expected_cost(order):
    none = np.cumprod(1 - p[list(order)])
    return float(np.sum(c[list(order)] * (1 - none)))

costs = {o: expected_cost(o) for o in permutations(range(3))}
for o, v in sorted(costs.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]):
    print(" -> ".join(names[i] for i in o), f"E[C] = {v:5.2f} s")
r = p / ((1 - p) * c)
print("order by increasing r:", " -> ".join(names[i] for i in np.argsort(r)))

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
changed = rng.random((10_000, 3)) < p                       # which steps change, per commit
def simulate(order):
    ch = changed[:, list(order)]
    first = np.where(ch.any(1), ch.argmax(1), 3)              # first changed position (3 = none)
    cc = c[list(order)]
    return float(np.mean([cc[f:].sum() for f in first]))
for o in [(0, 1, 2), (2, 1, 0)]:
    print(" -> ".join(names[i] for i in o), f"formula {costs[o]:.2f} s, simulation {simulate(o):.2f} s")
```
The sorted order (install, train, code) is the best of the six, and the
simulation agrees with the formula within sampling error. With these numbers
the reverse order costs many times more per commit: over a day of commits the
difference is minutes of waiting, multiplied by every developer and by CI.
(c) was checked by @exr-ctr1-build-medium: a code change rebuilds almost
nothing in order A and everything in order B. (d):
```{python}
#| output: asis
d = cb.scoring("multistage", dockerfile="""
    ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim
    FROM ${BASE} AS build
    WORKDIR /app
    COPY requirements.txt .
    RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --target=/deps -r requirements.txt \\
     && find /deps \\( -name tests -o -name __pycache__ \\) -type d -prune -exec rm -rf {} +
    ENV PYTHONPATH=/deps
    COPY train.py .
    RUN python train.py

    FROM ${BASE}
    COPY --from=build /deps /deps
    ENV PYTHONPATH=/deps
    WORKDIR /app
    COPY --from=build /app/model.joblib /app/model.json ./
    COPY serve.py score.py ./
    EXPOSE 8000
    CMD ["python", "serve.py"]
""", show_files=("Dockerfile",))
cb.build(d, "local/scoring:multi", table=False)
single = sum(l["size"] for l in cb.layers("local/scoring:1"))
multi = sum(l["size"] for l in cb.layers("local/scoring:multi"))
base = sum(l["size"] for l in cb.layers(cb.LOCAL["python"]))
print(cb._output_block(f"single stage: {single / 1e6:.0f} MB, multi-stage: {multi / 1e6:.0f} MB "
                       f"(base image {base / 1e6:.0f} MB; added on top: {(single - base) / 1e6:.0f} MB vs {(multi - base) / 1e6:.0f} MB)"))
cb.sh("docker run --rm local/scoring:multi python -c \"import sklearn, json; print(sklearn.__version__, json.load(open('model.json')))\"")
```
What the build adds on top of the base shrinks by about a quarter: the test
suites of the numerical libraries and the bytecode caches stay in the build
stage, and so do the training script and anything used to train. The image as
a whole shrinks less, because the base and the compiled libraries dominate it;
the larger wins come from slimmer bases (a `slim` or "distroless" base
instead of a full distribution) and, for compiled programs, from `FROM
scratch`. A first attempt that copied a virtual environment between the
stages made the image *larger* on this machine — the environment brings its
own `pip` — a reminder to measure rather than assume. Mistakes to avoid:
copying packages between stages whose Python versions differ (compiled
extensions are built for one version — both stages use the same `BASE`
here), and forgetting that the model file is in the build stage's working
directory.
:::

## Running containers {#sec-ctr-run}

### Life cycle

`docker run` is two operations: **create** (prepare the writable layer, the
namespaces and the cgroup) and **start** (start the process). A container is
then *running* until its main process exits, when it becomes *exited*; it
keeps its writable layer and its logs until it is **removed** (`docker rm`,
or automatically with `--rm`). `docker stop` asks the process to terminate,
`docker kill` forces it, and a **restart policy** (`--restart
on-failure`, `unless-stopped`) makes the engine start it again when it exits.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-ctr-lifecycle
%%| fig-cap: "States of a container and the commands that move between them. The main process defines the container: when it exits, the container stops."
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> created: docker create
  created --> running: docker start
  running --> exited: main process ends / docker stop / docker kill
  running --> paused: docker pause
  paused --> running: docker unpause
  exited --> running: docker start / restart policy
  exited --> [*]: docker rm
```

### Ports, environment and volumes

A container has its own network namespace, so a server listening on port 8000
inside is unreachable from the host until the port is **published**: `-p
8080:8000` asks the engine to forward the host's port 8080 to the container's
8000. Configuration enters through **environment variables** (`-e
PORT=9000`), which keeps one image valid for every environment — development,
test, production — as the twelve-factor methodology recommends
[@wiggins2011]. Here is the scoring service in action:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cb.reset_ids()
cb.run("docker rm -f scoring1 >/dev/null 2>&1")
cb.sh("docker run -d --name scoring1 -p 8080:8000 local/scoring:1")
time.sleep(3)
cb.sh("curl -s localhost:8080/version")
_wine = "[13.2, 1.78, 2.14, 11.2, 100, 2.65, 2.76, 0.26, 1.28, 4.38, 1.05, 3.4, 1050]"
cb.sh(f"curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/predict -d '{{\"features\": [{_wine}]}}'")
cb.sh("docker logs scoring1")
```

The files a container writes go to its writable layer and disappear with the
container. Data that must outlive it go to a **volume**: a **named volume**
(`-v models:/data`, a directory managed by the engine) or a **bind mount**
(`-v /host/path:/data`, a directory of the host). Volumes bypass the union
filesystem, so they are also faster for heavy I/O. Adding `:ro` makes a mount
read-only.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cb.run("docker volume rm -f notes >/dev/null 2>&1")
_u = cb.LOCAL["ubuntu"]
cb.sh(f"docker run --rm {_u} sh -c 'echo first > /note.txt' && docker run --rm {_u} cat /note.txt",
      shown="docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 sh -c 'echo first > /note.txt' && docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 cat /note.txt")
cb.sh(f"docker run --rm -v notes:/data {_u} sh -c 'echo kept > /data/note.txt' && docker run --rm -v notes:/data {_u} cat /data/note.txt",
      shown="docker run --rm -v notes:/data ubuntu:24.04 sh -c 'echo kept > /data/note.txt' && "
            "docker run --rm -v notes:/data ubuntu:24.04 cat /data/note.txt")
```

### Users and privileges

Unless told otherwise, the process in a container runs as **root**, and
without a user namespace (Docker does not create one by default) that is the
host's root, restricted by the other namespaces, by a reduced set of
