**capabilities** and by a seccomp filter of forbidden system calls — strong
restrictions, but a kernel vulnerability or a careless bind mount (`-v
/:/host`) turns them into full control of the host. Defence in depth means
removing what is not needed: a non-root user (`USER` in the Dockerfile or
`--user`), a read-only root filesystem (`--read-only`, with a `--tmpfs /tmp`
if the program needs scratch space), `--cap-drop ALL`,
`--security-opt no-new-privileges`, and limits on memory, CPU and processes
so that one container cannot starve the others (@thm-ctr-cpu-share). Rootless
Docker and Podman go further and run the whole engine as an ordinary user,
with root inside mapped to an unprivileged user outside.

### Signals, PID 1 and stopping

`docker stop` sends `SIGTERM` to the container's main process, waits (10
seconds by default, `-t` to change it) and then sends `SIGKILL`. A
well-behaved program catches `SIGTERM`, finishes the requests in progress,
closes files and exits — the *graceful shutdown* that orchestrators rely on
at every update. Part II showed how processes end and how signals work
(@sec-terminating, @sec-exit-status); containers add one twist.

::: {#prp-ctr-pid1}
## PID 1 ignores signals it does not handle
In a PID namespace, the kernel delivers to the namespace's first process
(PID 1) only the signals for which it has installed a handler; signals whose
action would be the default — such as termination by `SIGTERM` — are
discarded. (`SIGKILL` and `SIGSTOP` sent from an ancestor namespace are the
exception.) [@linuxmanpages2025, pid_namespaces(7)]
:::

*In one line:* a program that relies on the default action of `SIGTERM`
dies when run normally but **ignores** `docker stop` when it is PID 1, and is
killed only after the timeout.

This is the kernel's protection of `init`: on a normal system, PID 1 must not
be killed by accident. The consequences for containers:

- **Shell form** (`CMD python serve.py`) runs `/bin/sh -c "python serve.py"`:
  the shell is PID 1, has no handler, and does not forward the signal to
  Python. Use the **exec form** (`CMD ["python", "serve.py"]`), so that the
  program itself is PID 1, or `exec` in wrapper scripts.
- A program that is PID 1 must **handle `SIGTERM`** explicitly (the scoring
  server does, with `signal.signal`), or run under a tiny init process that
  forwards signals and reaps zombie processes: `docker run --init` adds one
  (`tini`).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
_s = time.perf_counter(); cb.run("docker stop scoring1"); stop_s = time.perf_counter() - _s
cb.sh("docker inspect -f 'status {{.State.Status}}, exit code {{.State.ExitCode}}' scoring1",
      shown="docker stop scoring1 && docker inspect -f 'status {{.State.Status}}, exit code {{.State.ExitCode}}' scoring1")
print(f"\n`docker stop` returned after {stop_s:.2f} s.\n")
cb.run("docker rm scoring1")
```

The scoring server handles `SIGTERM` and exits with status 0 well within the
timeout; @exr-ctr1-run-medium measures what happens otherwise.

### Exit codes

When the main process ends, the container's **exit code** is its exit
status, with the shell convention of Part II for deaths by signal: $128 + n$
for signal $n$ (@sec-exit-status, [@posix2024]). The codes met most often:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | normal termination |
| 1, 2, … | errors reported by the program itself |
| 125 | the `docker run` command itself failed (bad option) |
| 126 | the command could not be executed (permissions) |
| 127 | the command was not found |
| 137 = 128 + 9 | killed by `SIGKILL`: `docker kill`, the end of a `docker stop` timeout, or the **OOM killer** (@sec-ctr-kernel) |
| 143 = 128 + 15 | terminated by `SIGTERM` (the program did not catch it) |

::: {#prp-ctr-137}
## 137 does not prove a kill
An exit code of $128 + n$ is compatible both with death by signal $n$ and with
a normal exit with status $128 + n$.
:::

*In one line:* exit codes form one byte, and the convention shares it between
two meanings — to know whether the kernel's OOM killer intervened, ask the
engine, not the number.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ctr-137
`exit(c)` delivers $c \bmod 256$ to the parent (@prp-exit-status), so any
value in $0, \dots, 255$, including $128 + n$ for $n \le 127$, can be a
normal exit status. A container whose command is `sh -c 'exit 137'` ends
normally with 137:
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cb.reset_ids()
cb.run("docker rm -f fake137 >/dev/null 2>&1")
cb.sh(f"docker run --name fake137 {cb.LOCAL['ubuntu']} sh -c 'exit 137'; "
      "docker inspect -f 'exit code {{.State.ExitCode}}, OOMKilled {{.State.OOMKilled}}' fake137",
      shown="docker run --name fake137 ubuntu:24.04 sh -c 'exit 137'; "
            "docker inspect -f 'exit code {{.State.ExitCode}}, OOMKilled {{.State.OOMKilled}}' fake137", status=False)
cb.run("docker rm fake137")
```
The map from "how the process ended" to the code is therefore not injective,
and the code alone cannot identify the cause. $\blacksquare$
:::

Docker records the cause separately: `State.OOMKilled` is true when the
memory controller killed the process, and Kubernetes reports the reason
`OOMKilled` in the pod's status. Read those, not the number.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ctr1-run-easy}
## Easy — read the exit codes
Classify the exit codes 0, 1, 2, 126, 127, 130, 137, 139 and 143 of a
container: normal end, error reported by the program, failure to start, or
death by a signal — and in that case which signal, and a plausible cause.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Subtract 128 from the codes above 128 and look up the signal number (`kill
-l`, or Python's `signal.Signals`).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
import signal
for code in (0, 1, 2, 126, 127, 130, 137, 139, 143):
    if code > 128:
        sig = signal.Signals(code - 128)
        print(f"{code}: signal {code - 128} ({sig.name})")
    else:
        print(f"{code}: " + {0: "normal end", 1: "error reported by the program", 2: "error (often: wrong usage)",
                             126: "command found but not executable", 127: "command not found"}[code])
```
130 is `SIGINT` (Ctrl-C in an interactive container), 137 `SIGKILL`
(`docker kill`, a stop timeout, or the OOM killer — check `OOMKilled`), 139
`SIGSEGV` (a segmentation fault, as in Part II's out-of-bounds accesses), 143
`SIGTERM` not caught. Two cautions: a program may exit with any of these
numbers on purpose (@prp-ctr-137), and the 128 offset is a convention of
shells and engines — Python's `subprocess` reports a death by signal as a
negative `returncode` instead (@sec-exit-status).
:::

::: {#exr-ctr1-run-medium}
## Medium — the ten-second stop
Write a Python program that prints a line and then sleeps in a loop, without
any signal handling. Measure how long `docker stop` takes and which exit code
results when it runs (a) with the exec form, (b) with the shell form. Then fix
it in two ways — (c) with `--init`, (d) with a `SIGTERM` handler — and measure
again.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Run each variant with `docker run -d`, wait a second so that the program is
running, then time `docker stop`. @prp-ctr-pid1 predicts (a) and (b).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
d = cb.project("pid1")
cb.write(d, "sleeper.py", '''
    import time
    print("working", flush=True)
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
''')
cb.write(d, "polite.py", '''
    import signal, sys, time
    signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, lambda *_: sys.exit(0))   # finish cleanly on SIGTERM
    print("working", flush=True)
    while True:
        time.sleep(1)
''')
variants = {
    "(a) exec form, no handler":  "python /w/sleeper.py",
    "(b) shell form, no handler": "sh -c 'python /w/sleeper.py'",
    "(c) --init, no handler":     "--init python /w/sleeper.py",
    "(d) exec form, handler":     "python /w/polite.py",
}
img = cb.LOCAL["python"]
for label, cmd in variants.items():
    flags, cmd = ("--init", cmd[7:]) if cmd.startswith("--init") else ("", cmd)
    cb.run(f"docker rm -f stopme >/dev/null 2>&1; docker run -d --name stopme {flags} -v {d}:/w:ro {img} {cmd}")
    time.sleep(1.5)
    s = time.perf_counter(); cb.run("docker stop stopme"); t = time.perf_counter() - s
    code = cb.run("docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}}' stopme").stdout.strip()
    print(f"{label:28s} docker stop took {t:5.2f} s, exit code {code}")
cb.quiet("docker rm -f stopme")
```
(a) and (b) ignore `SIGTERM` (Python, or the shell, is PID 1 without a
handler for it), so `docker stop` waits the full timeout and then kills: 137.
With `--init`, `tini` is PID 1, forwards `SIGTERM` to Python, which is not
PID 1 and dies by the default action: fast, and 143. With the handler, Python
exits normally: fast, and 0 — the best outcome, because the program decides
what "cleanly" means. The ten seconds are not only a nuisance: during an
update, an orchestrator waits for them for every replica, and a process
killed by `SIGKILL` cannot flush buffers or finish requests. Mistake to
avoid: testing the handler with `python app.py` in a terminal, where the
program is not PID 1 and dies by default — the bug appears only in the
container.
:::

::: {#exr-ctr1-run-hard}
## Hard — a locked-down batch scorer
Run the scoring image as a **batch job**: score a CSV of wine measurements
mounted read-only from the host and write the predictions to a second mount,
as a non-root user (UID 10001), with a read-only root filesystem and a memory
limit of 128 MiB. Then feed it a file of one million rows: what happens, how
do you know, and how would you fix the program rather than the limit?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Use `--user 10001 --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --memory 128m --memory-swap 128m`
and two `-v host:container[:ro]` mounts. The output directory on the host
must be writable by UID 10001. `score.py` reads the whole file into Python
lists: estimate their size (a Python float is 24 bytes, plus 8 bytes per list
slot).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
import csv, os

d = cb.project("batch")
(d / "in").mkdir(); (d / "out").mkdir()
os.chown(d / "out", 10001, 10001)                     # the container's user must be able to write
Xw = load_wine().data
with open(d / "in" / "wines.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    csv.writer(f).writerows(Xw.round(4).tolist())

def score(extra=""):
    cmd = (f"docker run --rm --user 10001 --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --memory 128m --memory-swap 128m "
           f"-v {d}/in:/data/in:ro -v {d}/out:/data/out --name batch {extra} local/scoring:1 python score.py")
    p = cb.run(cmd)
    return p.returncode, cb.mask(p.stdout + p.stderr).strip()[-300:]

print(score())
print("first predictions:", (d / "out" / "wines.csv").read_text().split()[:10])

big = np.tile(Xw, (1_000_000 // len(Xw) + 1, 1))[:1_000_000]
with open(d / "in" / "wines.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    csv.writer(f).writerows(big.round(4).tolist())
print(f"input file: {(d / 'in' / 'wines.csv').stat().st_size / 1e6:.0f} MB")
cb.run("docker rm -f batch-oom >/dev/null 2>&1")
p = cb.run(f"docker run --user 10001 --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --memory 128m --memory-swap 128m "
           f"-v {d}/in:/data/in:ro -v {d}/out:/data/out --name batch-oom local/scoring:1 python score.py")
state = cb.run("docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' batch-oom").stdout.split()
print(f"one million rows: exit code {state[0]}, OOMKilled {state[1]}")
cb.quiet("docker rm batch-oom")
```
The small file is scored without any write outside the output mount: the
container cannot modify its own filesystem, cannot read anything of the host
but its input, and its process is not root. The large file kills it: exit
code 137 with `OOMKilled` true — the kernel's memory controller, not a bug
in Python's error handling, ended it, which is why there is no traceback.
The cause is the design of `score.py`: one million rows of 13 numbers as
Python lists take about $10^6 \times 13 \times (24 + 8) \approx 420$ MB,
far more than the limit, before scikit-learn even sees them. The fix is to
**stream**: read and predict in chunks of, say, 10 000 rows, so that memory
is bounded by the chunk size whatever the file size:
```{python}
cb.write(d, "score_stream.py", '''
    import csv, itertools, os
    from pathlib import Path
    import joblib, numpy as np
    model = joblib.load("/app/model.joblib")
    src, dst = Path("/data/in"), Path("/data/out")
    for path in sorted(src.glob("*.csv")):
        n = 0
        with path.open() as fin, (dst / path.name).open("w", newline="") as fout:
            rows, out = csv.reader(fin), csv.writer(fout)
            while chunk := list(itertools.islice(rows, 10_000)):       # at most 10 000 rows in memory
                X = np.asarray(chunk, dtype=float)
                out.writerows([[int(p)] for p in model.predict(X)])
                n += len(chunk)
        print(f"{path.name}: {n} rows scored")
''')
p = cb.run(f"docker run --rm --user 10001 --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --memory 128m --memory-swap 128m "
           f"-v {d}/in:/data/in:ro -v {d}/out:/data/out -v {d}/score_stream.py:/app/score_stream.py:ro "
           f"local/scoring:1 python score_stream.py")
print(p.returncode, p.stdout.strip())
```
Same container, same limit, one million rows scored. Raising the limit would
only move the failure to the next, larger file. Typical mistakes: a host
output directory owned by root (the non-root user gets `PermissionError`),
forgetting `--memory-swap` (with swap the process slows down instead of being
killed, which hides the problem), and reading the 137 as "the program
crashed".
:::

## Orchestrating with Kubernetes {#sec-ctr-k8s}

### Desired state and control loops

Kubernetes manages a **cluster**: a set of machines (*nodes*) and a
**control plane** — an API server that stores every object in a key–value
database (etcd), a **scheduler** that assigns new pods to nodes, and
**controllers** that run control loops [@burns2016; @kubernetes2026]. On
every node a **kubelet** asks the container runtime to run the containers
assigned to it (@fig-ctr-stack). The user never says "start this container on
that machine"; they submit **objects** that describe a desired state:

| Object | Describes |
|---|---|
| **Pod** | one or more containers that run together on one node, share a network namespace (one IP address) and possibly volumes; the unit of scheduling |
| **ReplicaSet** | "keep $R$ pods matching this label selector and this template running" |
| **Deployment** | a ReplicaSet plus a **rollout** strategy for replacing it with a new one |
| **Service** | a stable name and virtual IP that load-balances over the ready pods matching a selector |
| **ConfigMap**, **Secret** | configuration and credentials injected as environment variables or files |

Each controller is a **reconciliation loop**: observe the actual state, compare
it with the desired one, act to reduce the difference, repeat. The loop does
not remember *how* the gap appeared — a crash, a deleted pod, a lost node, a
changed manifest are all the same to it — which is what makes the system
robust: there is one mechanism for every failure.

### A deployment of the scoring service

```{python}
#| echo: false
cb.ensure_k3s()
k8s_version = json.loads(cb.kube_run("version -o json").stdout)["serverVersion"]["gitVersion"].split("+")[0]
```

The cluster used here is a single-node **k3s** [@k3s2026], a compact
Kubernetes distribution, running Kubernetes `{python} k8s_version` on the
build machine. With no registry reachable, the image is copied
directly into the node's container store; in a real cluster the image would be
pushed to a registry and pulled by each node.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cb.kube_run("delete deployment scoring --ignore-not-found --wait=true")
cb.kube_run("delete service scoring --ignore-not-found")
cb.load_image("local/scoring:1")
d = cb.project("k8s")
cb.show(d, "scoring.yaml", """
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    metadata:
      name: scoring
    spec:
      replicas: 3
      selector:
        matchLabels: {app: scoring}
      strategy:
        type: RollingUpdate
        rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0}
      template:
        metadata:
          labels: {app: scoring}
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: web
            image: local/scoring:1
            imagePullPolicy: Never          # loaded into the node: no registry in this book
            ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
            env: [{name: STARTUP_DELAY, value: "3"}]
            readinessProbe:                 # receive traffic only once /health answers
              httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8000}
              periodSeconds: 1
            resources:
              requests: {cpu: 250m, memory: 128Mi}
              limits: {cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi}
    ---
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Service
    metadata:
      name: scoring
    spec:
      type: NodePort
      selector: {app: scoring}
      ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 8000, nodePort: 30080}]
""")
cb.kube("apply -f scoring.yaml", cwd=d)
cb.kube("rollout status deployment/scoring --timeout=120s")
_cols = "-o custom-columns=POD:.metadata.name,READY:.status.containerStatuses[0].ready,PHASE:.status.phase"
cb.kube(f"get pods -l app=scoring {_cols}")
```

The `STARTUP_DELAY` variable makes each server wait three seconds before
loading the model — a stand-in for a large model that takes time to load —
and the **readiness probe** keeps a pod out of the Service until its
`/health` answers. Requests to the node's port 30080 are spread over the
ready pods:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
time.sleep(2)
cb.sh("for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl -s localhost:30080/health; echo; done | sort | uniq -c")
```

The `resources` of the manifest are cgroup settings in disguise
(@sec-ctr-kernel): **requests** are what the scheduler reserves on a node and
become the CPU weight; **limits** become the quota and the memory cap.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
cb.kube(f"exec deploy/scoring -- sh -c '{_probe}'")
```

A CPU limit of `500m` (half a CPU) is a quota of 50 000 µs per 100 000 µs;
the memory limit is $256 \times 2^{20}$ bytes; the CPU request of `250m` became
the v1 share $256 = 250 \times 1024/1000$ (on v2, a weight).

**Self-healing.** Delete a pod, as a crash or the loss of a node would:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
_victim = cb.kube_run("get pods -l app=scoring -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}'").stdout.strip()
cb.kube(f"delete pod {_victim} --wait=false", shown="kubectl delete pod <one of the three> --wait=false")
time.sleep(1)
cb.kube(f"get pods -l app=scoring {_cols}")
cb.kube_run("rollout status deployment/scoring --timeout=120s")
time.sleep(2)
cb.kube(f"get pods -l app=scoring {_cols}")
```

The ReplicaSet controller saw two pods where three were desired and created a
third, which joined the Service once ready. **Scaling** is a change of the
desired number (`kubectl scale deployment/scoring --replicas=5`), and a
**HorizontalPodAutoscaler** changes it automatically from a measured metric.

### Rolling updates

A new version of the model is a new image. Changing the Deployment's template
starts a **rolling update**: a new ReplicaSet is created and scaled up while
the old one is scaled down, within two bounds — **maxSurge** (how many pods
above the desired number may exist) and **maxUnavailable** (how many below it
may be unready). Percentages are converted to numbers by rounding the surge up
and the unavailability down [@kubernetes2026, "Deployments"].

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
d2 = cb.scoring("scoring-v2", version="2")
cb.build(d2, "local/scoring:2", table=False, show_cmd=False)
cb.load_image("local/scoring:2")
_s = time.perf_counter()
cb.kube("set image deployment/scoring web=local/scoring:2")
cb.kube("rollout status deployment/scoring --timeout=180s", filter_fn=lambda l: "successfully" in l)
rollout_s = time.perf_counter() - _s
for _ in range(30):                                   # kube-proxy updates its rules a moment later
    if '"version": "2"' in cb.run("curl -s localhost:30080/version").stdout:
        break
    time.sleep(0.5)
cb.sh("curl -s localhost:30080/version")
```

With three replicas, `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0`, the controller
can only add one new pod at a time and must wait until it is ready before
removing an old one. The update took `{python} f"{rollout_s:.0f}"` s here; the next
result explains why it cannot take much less.

::: {#prp-ctr-rollout}
## Bounds of a rolling update
Let $R$ be the desired number of replicas, $s$ the surge and $u$ the
unavailability allowed (after rounding), with $s + u \ge 1$. During a rolling
update, at every moment (i) at most $R + s$ pods exist and (ii) at least $R -
u$ pods are ready. Consequently (iii) at most $s + u$ pods are starting at
any moment, and if every new pod needs a time $T$ from creation to
readiness, the update takes at least $\lceil R/(s + u)\rceil\, T$.
:::

*In one line:* the update proceeds in waves of at most $s + u$ pods, so its
duration is at least the number of waves times the start-up time — a slow
model load makes every deployment slow.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ctr-rollout
(i) and (ii) are the invariants the Deployment controller maintains: it
scales the new ReplicaSet up only while the total stays $\le R + s$, and the
old one down only while the ready pods stay $\ge R - u$ [@kubernetes2026,
"Deployments"]. (iii) A pod that is starting exists but is not ready, so
their number is at most (pods existing) $-$ (pods ready) $\le (R + s) - (R -
u) = s + u$. All $R$ new pods must go through a starting period of length $T$;
in any time window of length $T$ at most $s + u$ pods can *complete* their
start (each must have been starting during the whole window, and at most $s +
u$ start in parallel). Covering $R$ completions needs at least $\lceil R/(s +
u)\rceil$ windows. $\blacksquare$
:::

Here $R = 3$, $s = 1$, $u = 0$ and $T \approx 3$–4 s (the delay, the model load
and the probe period), so at least $3 \times T \approx 9$–12 s, consistent with
the measured `{python} f"{rollout_s:.0f}"` s, which also includes the scheduling and the
termination of the old pods. Raising $u$ speeds the update up at the cost of
capacity; raising $s$ speeds it up at the cost of extra resources.

### Autoscaling and scheduling

The **HorizontalPodAutoscaler** periodically sets the number of replicas from
a metric $m$ (for instance the average CPU utilisation of the pods, relative to
their request) and a target $t$:
$$
R' = \left\lceil R\,\frac{m}{t}\right\rceil ,
$$ {#eq-ctr-hpa}
and does nothing when $m/t$ is within a tolerance (by default 0.1) of 1
[@kubernetes2026, "Horizontal Pod Autoscaling"].

::: {#prp-ctr-hpa}
## The proportional rule reaches its fixed point in one step
Suppose the total load $L$ is spread evenly, so that with $R$ replicas the
per-pod metric is $m = L/R$. Then from any $R$ the rule @eq-ctr-hpa gives
$R' = \lceil L/t\rceil$, and $R^* = \lceil L/t\rceil$ is a fixed point: once
there, the rule keeps it.
:::

*In one line:* the replicas times the per-pod load is the total load, so the
rule computes directly how many pods the load needs at the target
utilisation.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ctr-hpa
$R\,m/t = R\,(L/R)/t = L/t$, independent of $R$, so $R' = \lceil L/t\rceil$.
Applying the rule at $R^*$ gives $\lceil L/t\rceil = R^*$ again. (The
tolerance only adds states where the rule does not move; real loads are not
perfectly even and change over time, which is why the controller also limits
how fast it scales and waits five minutes before scaling down.)
$\blacksquare$
:::

Finally, the **scheduler** places each new pod on a node whose free
allocatable resources cover the pod's **requests**, choosing among the
feasible nodes by a score (spreading, packing, affinity). Choosing placements
that use the fewest nodes is bin packing, an NP-hard problem [@garey1979], so
the scheduler uses greedy rules pod by pod rather than an optimum.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ctr1-k8s-easy}
## Easy — rollout and autoscaling by hand
(a) A Deployment has 10 replicas and the default `maxSurge: 25%`,
`maxUnavailable: 25%`. How many pods can exist at most during an update, how
many must stay ready, and how many waves does the update need at least? (b)
With 4 replicas, `maxSurge: 1`, `maxUnavailable: 0`, and pods that need 20 s
to load the model, what is the minimum duration of an update? (c) Four pods
run at an average CPU utilisation of 90 % with a target of 60 %: how many does
the autoscaler ask for? If the load stays the same, what happens at the next
evaluation?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Round the surge up and the unavailability down; then apply
@prp-ctr-rollout and @eq-ctr-hpa. For the second evaluation, the per-pod
utilisation is the total load divided by the new number of pods.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) $s = \lceil 2.5\rceil = 3$, $u = \lfloor 2.5\rfloor = 2$: at most 13 pods,
at least 8 ready, at least $\lceil 10/5\rceil = 2$ waves. (b) $\lceil
4/1\rceil \times 20 = 80$ s at least. (c) $\lceil 4 \times 90/60\rceil = 6$;
the total load is $4 \times 90 = 360$ "percent-pods", so with 6 pods each runs
at 60 %, $m/t = 1$, and the autoscaler stays at 6 (@prp-ctr-hpa).
```{python}
import math
R, s, u = 10, math.ceil(0.25 * 10), math.floor(0.25 * 10)
print(f"(a) at most {R + s} pods, at least {R - u} ready, at least {math.ceil(R / (s + u))} waves")
print(f"(b) at least {math.ceil(4 / 1) * 20} s")
R1 = math.ceil(4 * 90 / 60); m1 = 4 * 90 / R1
print(f"(c) {R1} pods; then utilisation {m1:.0f}% -> {math.ceil(R1 * m1 / 60)} pods")
```
The common slip in (a) is rounding both percentages the same way; the
asymmetry is deliberate, so that the update always makes progress ($s + u
\ge 1$) and never breaks availability more than allowed.
:::

::: {#exr-ctr1-k8s-medium}
## Medium — a reconciliation loop of your own
Write a minimal controller in Python on top of Docker: given a desired state
`{"app": "scoring", "image": "local/scoring:1", "replicas": 3}`, each
iteration lists the running containers labelled `app=scoring`, starts or
removes containers to match the desired number, and logs its actions. Run a
few iterations, kill one container by hand between two of them, then change
the desired number of replicas.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`docker run -d --label app=scoring ...` and `docker ps -q --filter
label=app=scoring` give you a selector; exited containers should be removed
(`docker ps -aq --filter status=exited`). The controller must be idempotent:
running an iteration twice on the same state does nothing the second time.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
def observe(app):
    """IDs of the running and of the dead containers of an app."""
    running = cb.run(f"docker ps -q --filter label=app={app}").stdout.split()
    dead = cb.run(f"docker ps -aq --filter label=app={app} --filter status=exited").stdout.split()
    return running, dead

def reconcile(desired):
    app, image, want = desired["app"], desired["image"], desired["replicas"]
    running, dead = observe(app)
    actions = []
    for cid in dead:                                           # clean up what died
        cb.run(f"docker rm {cid}"); actions.append("removed a dead container")
    for _ in range(want - len(running)):                      # too few: start
        cb.run(f"docker run -d --label app={app} {image}"); actions.append("started a container")
    for cid in running[want:]:                                # too many: stop the extra ones
        cb.run(f"docker rm -f {cid}"); actions.append("removed a surplus container")
    return actions or ["nothing to do"]

desired = {"app": "scoring", "image": "local/scoring:1", "replicas": 3}
cb.run("docker rm -f $(docker ps -aq --filter label=app=scoring) 2>/dev/null")
for step in range(6):
    if step == 2:                                             # a "crash": kill one container
        victim = observe("scoring")[0][0]
        cb.run(f"docker kill {victim}"); print("   ** killed one container by hand")
    if step == 4:
        desired["replicas"] = 2;  print("   ** desired replicas changed to 2")
    print(f"iteration {step}: {', '.join(reconcile(desired))}; running now: {len(observe('scoring')[0])}")
    time.sleep(1)
cb.quiet("docker rm -f $(docker ps -aq --filter label=app=scoring) 2>/dev/null")
```
The controller does not know *why* the state differs from the desired one —
it compares and acts — and an iteration on a converged state does nothing
(idempotence), so running it periodically is safe. Real controllers add what
this one lacks: they watch the API instead of polling, act on a cache of the
state, use the generation number to avoid acting twice on the same change,
and handle partial failures (a container that cannot start would make this
loop start one at every iteration — Kubernetes backs off exponentially, the
`CrashLoopBackOff` state). A classic mistake is a loop that is not idempotent,
e.g. "start one container per iteration while fewer than 3 exist" without
re-observing: two fast iterations overshoot.
:::

::: {#exr-ctr1-k8s-hard}
## Hard — an update without a dropped request
While a client sends a steady stream of prediction requests to the Service,
roll the Deployment from version 1 to version 2 and count the failed requests.
Do it twice: (a) with the readiness probe and `maxUnavailable: 0` as above;
(b) without the readiness probe. Explain the difference, and what else can
still drop requests when a pod is terminated.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Run the client in a thread: new connection per request, short timeout, record
successes and failures until the rollout finishes. Without a readiness
probe, a pod counts as ready as soon as its container has started — before
the server listens. Removing a pod from the Service and sending it `SIGTERM`
happen in parallel.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
import http.client, threading

BODY = json.dumps({"features": [[13.2, 1.78, 2.14, 11.2, 100, 2.65, 2.76, 0.26, 1.28, 4.38, 1.05, 3.4, 1050]]})

def client(stop, results):
    while not stop.is_set():
        try:
            c = http.client.HTTPConnection("127.0.0.1", 30080, timeout=2)
            c.request("POST", "/predict", BODY, {"Content-Type": "application/json"})
            ok = c.getresponse().status == 200
            c.close()
        except OSError:
            ok = False
        results.append(ok)
        time.sleep(0.02)

def rollout(to_image, probe):
    patch = [{"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/template/spec/containers/0/image", "value": to_image}]
    if not probe:
        patch.append({"op": "remove", "path": "/spec/template/spec/containers/0/readinessProbe"})
    stop, results = threading.Event(), []
    t = threading.Thread(target=client, args=(stop, results)); t.start()
    time.sleep(2)                                               # steady state before the update
    cb.kube_run(f"patch deployment scoring --type=json -p '{json.dumps(patch)}'")
    cb.kube_run("rollout status deployment/scoring --timeout=180s")
    time.sleep(2)
    stop.set(); t.join()
    return len(results), results.count(False)

cb.kube_run("rollout status deployment/scoring --timeout=120s")         # currently version 2, with probe
n_a, bad_a = rollout("local/scoring:1", probe=True)
print(f"(a) with readiness probe:    {n_a} requests, {bad_a} failed")
n_b, bad_b = rollout("local/scoring:2", probe=False)
print(f"(b) without readiness probe: {n_b} requests, {bad_b} failed")
```
With the probe, the new pods receive traffic only once they answer, and with
`maxUnavailable: 0` the old ones are removed only after that: only
`{python} f"{100 * bad_a / n_a:.1f}"` % of the requests failed. Without the
probe, each new pod is declared ready the moment its container starts, the
Service sends it requests while the server is still loading, and the
connections are refused — a burst of failures at every wave, here
`{python} f"{100 * bad_b / n_b:.0f}"` % of the requests (fewer requests were
sent, because each failed one waited for its timeout). The residual failures that can remain even with the
probe come from termination: the endpoints controller removes the pod from
the Service *while* the pod receives `SIGTERM`, and for a short time some
nodes may still route to it. The standard remedies are a `preStop` hook that
sleeps a few seconds before the signal, and a server that, on `SIGTERM`,
stops accepting new connections but finishes the ones in progress. Mistakes to
avoid: measuring with a single client request per second (too coarse to see
the burst), and using a liveness probe for what a readiness probe should do —
a failing liveness probe *restarts* the container, which makes a slow start
slower.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
cb.quiet("k3s kubectl delete deployment scoring --wait=true", env=cb.K8S_ENV)
cb.quiet("k3s kubectl delete service scoring", env=cb.K8S_ENV)
```

::: {.project-link}
**In the projects.** This course has no final project, so the techniques of
the chapter are best tried on the projects of the earlier parts:

- **The phone book of Part I** (@sec-ch-project-phonebook) keeps its contacts
  in a JSON file. In a container that file must live on a **volume**, or every
  `docker rm` would lose the contacts; and since the program is interactive,
  it needs `-it`. With the project's modules in the build context and a
  two-line `run.py` that calls `main(sys.argv[1])`:
  ```dockerfile
  ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim
  FROM ${BASE}
  WORKDIR /app
  COPY . .
  USER 10001
  CMD ["python", "run.py", "/data/phonebook.json"]
  ```
  `docker run -it -v phonebook-data:/data phonebook` — and the atomic writes
  of @sec-atomic-writes keep working, because the temporary file and the
  target are on the same volume.
- **The CRM of Part II** (@sec-ch-project-crm) is a CMake project: a
  multi-stage build compiles it with the full toolchain and ships only the
  executable, linked statically, on an empty base, with its data folder on a
  volume:
  ```dockerfile
  ARG BUILDER=gcc:13
  FROM ${BUILDER} AS build
  RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends cmake ninja-build
  WORKDIR /src
  COPY . .
  RUN cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS=-static \
   && cmake --build build && ./build/crm_tests
  FROM scratch
  COPY --from=build /src/build/crm /crm
  ENTRYPOINT ["/crm", "/data"]
  ```
  Running the tests in the build stage means that an image is produced only
  if they pass.
- **The $k$-NN classifier of Part IV** (@sec-ch-mla-project) is served exactly
  like the wine model of this chapter: train in the build, `joblib.dump` the
  pipeline, load it in the server. Part VI gives it a proper API.
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **`latest` and other moving tags** in `FROM` or in deployments: the image
  changes under your feet. Pin versions, and digests for production.
- **Copying the whole project before installing dependencies**: every code
  change reinstalls everything (@thm-ctr-prefix).
- **Deleting in a later step what an earlier step added** — files, caches,
  secrets: the bytes stay in the image (@prp-ctr-size).
- **Secrets in the image**: in `COPY`, `ARG` or `ENV`. Use secret mounts at
  build time and secrets injected at run time.
- **Shell-form `CMD` and PID 1 without a `SIGTERM` handler**: ten-second stops,
  killed requests (@prp-ctr-pid1).
- **Data in the writable layer**: lost with the container. Use volumes.
- **Running as root** with a writable root filesystem and all capabilities.
- **No memory limit**, or a limit that only hides a design that loads
  everything into memory (@exr-ctr1-run-hard).
- **Reading 137 as "crashed"**: check `OOMKilled` (@prp-ctr-137).
- **No readiness probe**: traffic reaches pods that are still starting.
- **Assuming `--cpu-shares` ratios survive on cgroup v2**: the conversion is
  not proportional.
:::

## Summary

- A container is a process with a private view of the kernel's resources
  (**namespaces**), a root filesystem from an image (**`chroot`/`pivot_root`**
  over a **union filesystem**) and resource limits (**cgroups**); it shares the
  host's kernel, unlike a VM.
- Under contention, weighted fair, work-conserving scheduling gives each busy
  group $w_i/\sum_{A}w_j$ of the CPU; a quota caps a group at $q/P$ CPUs even
  on an idle machine.
- An OCI image is a Merkle DAG of SHA-256-addressed blobs; collisions are
  negligible (at most $\binom n2 2^{-256}$), so one digest identifies the whole
  image. Tags move; digests do not.
- Layers only add: deleting hides, never removes. Reproducible images need
  fixed timestamps and pinned inputs.
- The build cache has the prefix property; the expected rebuild cost is
  $\sum c_i[1 - \prod_{j \le i}(1 - p_j)]$ and is minimised by sorting steps
  by $p_i/((1 - p_i)c_i)$. Multi-stage builds ship only what is needed.
- PID 1 ignores unhandled signals; use the exec form, a `SIGTERM` handler or
  `--init`. Exit codes $128 + n$ mean "signal $n$" by convention only.
- Kubernetes reconciles desired and actual state with control loops;
  Deployments roll out in waves of at most $s + u$ pods, so they take at least
  $\lceil R/(s + u)\rceil T$; the autoscaler's proportional rule jumps to
  $\lceil L/t\rceil$ replicas.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-ctr1-reproducible}
**A reproducible batch scorer.** Write a Dockerfile for the batch scorer of
@exr-ctr1-run-hard (with the streaming `score_stream.py`) such that two
builds from scratch (`--no-cache`) give the **same image digest**. Prove it by
building twice, then use the image to score the wine data and compare the
predictions with those of the model trained on the host.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| output: asis
cb.reset_ids()
d = cb.scoring("reproducible", dockerfile="""
    ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim
    FROM ${BASE}
    ARG SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH
    ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
    WORKDIR /app
    COPY requirements.txt .
    RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --no-compile -r requirements.txt
    COPY train.py .
    RUN python train.py
    COPY score_stream.py .
    USER 10001
    CMD ["python", "score_stream.py"]
""", show_files=("Dockerfile",))
(d / "score_stream.py").write_text((cb.WORK / "batch" / "score_stream.py").read_text())
ids = []
for k in (1, 2):
    cb.build(d, f"local/batch:{k}", table=False, show_cmd=False,
             extra=f"--no-cache --provenance=false --build-arg SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=0 "
                   f"--output type=image,name=local/batch:{k},rewrite-timestamp=true")
    ids.append(cb.image_id(f"local/batch:{k}"))
print(cb._output_block(cb.mask(f"build 1: {ids[0]}\nbuild 2: {ids[1]}\nidentical: {ids[0] == ids[1]}")))
```
```{python}
db = cb.WORK / "batch"
with open(db / "in" / "wines.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    csv.writer(f).writerows(Xw.round(4).tolist())
p = cb.run(f"docker run --rm --read-only --memory 128m -v {db}/in:/data/in:ro -v {db}/out:/data/out local/batch:1")
print(p.stdout.strip())
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
host = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(*load_wine(return_X_y=True))
container_pred = np.loadtxt(db / "out" / "wines.csv", dtype=int)
host_pred = host.predict(np.loadtxt(db / "in" / "wines.csv", delimiter=","))
print("predictions identical to the model trained on the host:", np.array_equal(container_pred, host_pred))
```
Three ingredients make the digest repeatable: pinned inputs (the base image
is fixed here; the packages are pinned by version — add `--require-hashes` for
protection against a changed file on the index), deterministic steps (the
training uses a deterministic solver on fixed data; `--no-compile` and
`PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE` avoid `.pyc` files with timestamps), and fixed
metadata (`SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`, rewritten file timestamps, no provenance
attestation with build times). The predictions coincide with the host's
because the versions are the same — the point of pinning. On another machine,
the same digest is obtained only from the same base image digest: pin it in
`FROM`.
:::

::: {#exr-ctr1-pod}
**From `docker run` to a Pod.** Translate `docker run -d -p 8080:8000 -e
STARTUP_DELAY=0 --memory 256m --cpus 0.5 --user 10001 --read-only --tmpfs /tmp
local/scoring:1` into a Pod manifest (with a Service for the port), apply it,
and verify from inside the pod the user, the read-only root filesystem and the
cgroup limits.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| output: asis
d = cb.project("pod")
cb.show(d, "pod.yaml", """
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Pod
    metadata:
      name: scoring-pod
      labels: {app: scoring-pod}
    spec:
      securityContext: {runAsUser: 10001, runAsNonRoot: true}           # --user 10001
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: local/scoring:1
        imagePullPolicy: Never
        env: [{name: STARTUP_DELAY, value: "0"}]                          # -e
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
        securityContext: {readOnlyRootFilesystem: true}                   # --read-only
        resources:
          limits: {memory: 256Mi, cpu: 500m}                              # --memory, --cpus
        volumeMounts: [{name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}]
      volumes: [{name: tmp, emptyDir: {medium: Memory}}]                  # --tmpfs /tmp
    ---
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: Service
    metadata: {name: scoring-pod}
    spec:
      type: NodePort
      selector: {app: scoring-pod}
      ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 8000, nodePort: 30081}]              # -p (on the node)
""")
cb.kube_run("delete -f pod.yaml --ignore-not-found --wait=true", cwd=d)
cb.load_image("local/scoring:1")                     # make sure the node has the image (no registry here)
cb.kube("apply -f pod.yaml", cwd=d)
for _ in range(120):                                  # wait until the pod is scheduled and ready
    if cb.kube_run("get pod scoring-pod -o jsonpath={.status.containerStatuses[0].ready}").stdout == "true":
        break
    time.sleep(1)
cb.kube("exec scoring-pod -- sh -c 'id -u; touch /app/x 2>&1 | head -1; touch /tmp/ok && echo /tmp is writable'")
cb.kube(f"exec scoring-pod -- sh -c '{_probe}'")
time.sleep(1)
cb.sh("curl -s localhost:30081/version")
cb.kube_run("delete -f pod.yaml --wait=true", cwd=d)
```
Every flag has a field: `-e` → `env`, `--user` → `securityContext.runAsUser`,
`--read-only` → `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, `--tmpfs` → an `emptyDir` volume in
memory, `--memory` and `--cpus` → `resources.limits` (which become the same
cgroup files as with Docker), `-p` → a Service. The differences are as
instructive: there is no `-d` (pods always run in the background), there is no
`--rm` (the pod's life cycle is the controller's business), and a bare Pod,
unlike a Deployment, is not recreated if deleted — in practice one always uses
a Deployment (or a Job, for batch work such as @exr-ctr1-reproducible).
:::

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

- @kerrisk2010, ch. 20–22, 26 and 28 — signals, process termination, process
  creation; the man pages namespaces(7), pid_namespaces(7), user_namespaces(7)
  and cgroups(7) by the same author [@linuxmanpages2025] are the reference for
  @sec-ctr-kernel.
- @heo2015 — the cgroup v2 design and interface: "Weights", "Limits", the CPU
  and memory controllers.
- @parekh1993 — generalised processor sharing, the model behind
  @thm-ctr-cpu-share.
- @popek1974, @soltesz2007 and @felter2015 — virtual machines versus
  operating-system virtualisation, in theory and in measurements.
- @oci2025image and @oci2025runtime — the image format (manifest, index,
  layers, descriptors) and the runtime specification; @nist2015 for SHA-256;
  @merkle1987 for hash trees.
- @docker2026 — Dockerfile reference, build cache, multi-stage builds, build
  secrets; @reproduciblebuilds2017 — `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`.
- @verma2015 and @burns2016 — Borg and the lessons that shaped Kubernetes;
  @kubernetes2026 — concepts: Pods, Deployments, Services, probes, resource
  management, autoscaling.
- @merkel2014 — Docker as presented to developers in its first year.
